— Neighbor: A  system  is  called  a  neighbor  of  system A,  when  it  has  a  neighbor  relationship  with

system A.

— Interference victim: A system is an interference victim, when there is at least one BS or one SS in
the system that receives harmful interference from neighbor systems. The interference victim could
be an interference source to its neighbors at the same time (e.g., system A/B/C/D in Figure 15-1), or
only a victim of its neighbors (e.g., system F in Figure 15-2).

— Interference source: A system is an interference source, when there is at least one BS or one SS in
the system that causes harmful interference to its neighbor systems. The interference source could
be an interference victim of its neighbors at the same time (e.g., system A/B/C/D in Figure 15-1), or
only an interference source to its neighbors (e.g., system E in Figure 15-2).

— Interference  victim  BS/SS: A  BS/SS  in  an  interference  victim  system  when  the  BS/SS  receives
harmful  interference  from  one  or  more  SS/BS  transmitting  in  the  system’s  neighborhood.  The
interference victim system could be at the same time an interference source BS/SS to the SS/BS in
its neighborhood (e.g., BS in system A/B/C and the interference victim SSs in system A/B/C/D in
Figure 15-1), or only an interference victim BS/SS of the interference source SS/BS in its neighbor
system (e.g., interference victim BS/SS in System F in Figure 15-2).

— Interference source BS/SS: A BS/SS in an interference source system is an interference source BS/
SS  when  the  BS/SS  creates  harmful  interference  to  one  or  more  SS/BS  in  the  system’s  neighbor
system. The interference source BS/SS could be an interference victim BS/SS of the SS/BS in its
neighbor  system  at  the  same  time  (e.g.,  BS  in  system A/B/C  and  the  interference  source  SSs  in
system A/B/C/D in Figure 15-1), or only an interference source system of its neighbor system (e.g.,
Interference source BS/SS in system E in Figure 15-2).

— Interference neighborhood: An interference neighborhood relates to a specific system. A system
will  perceive  as  an  interference  neighbor  any  other  systems  to/from  which  it  creates/receives
harmful interference. Figure 15-3 shows some examples of neighborhood.

— Community:  A  community  is  composed  of  those  systems  that  coordinate  to  resolve  their

interference. These systems can be operated by the same or different operators.

15.1.3 Procedure in WirelessMAN-CX

15.1.3.1 Procedure flow for BS

In general, coexistence detection, avoidance, and resolution are performed in two stages—the initialization
stage and the operating stage. In bands where SSUs are present, the procedures described in 6.4.1.2 shall be
followed.

Initialization stage—This stage is described in 15.1.4.4.

a)
b) Operating stage—In the operating stage, the BS has SSs associated with it. The BS and its serving
SSs should monitor the channel status on the working channel and the non-working channels and
update  its  interference status in the information table  (Annex Q).  If interference  status  varies,  the
system  should  update its resource allocation  to  get an interference free  resource, and  at  the  same
time use the free bandwidth efficiently. The changes in interference status shall be triggered when a
primary  user  is  detected,  when  a  new  free  channel  is  found,  or  when  the  number  of  interference
neighbor systems varies.

The interference within subframes can be optimally assessed using CXCC.

If a new free channel is detected and the working channel of the system is too crowded, a system may switch
to the new free channel.

If a system has no interference neighbor and finds a new free channel, it should record the new free channel
as its alternative channel in the information table. The alternative channel may be used for the optimization
of channel distribution or fast channel switching when a primary user is detected on the working channel.
The  procedures  for  the  optimization  of  the  frequency  channels  distribution  are  described  in  15.4.2.
Alternately,  the  channel  switching  may  be  requested  by  another  BS/NCMN;  messages  over-the-air  and
primitives are provided as part of the CXP.

If  a  primary  user  is  detected  on  current  working  channel  and  a  system  is  not  allowed  to  share  the  same
channel with this user, the system shall stop working on that channel at the required switching time. At the
same  time,  a  system  should  try  to  find  free  working  bandwidth  for  itself,  as  a  free  channel  and/or  a  free
Master subframe, following the procedures described for the initialization stage.

There are two reasons for changes in the interference status. They are the addition of a new uncoordinated
interference system, and the release of an interference neighbor system. If a new interference BS or SS is
identified,  a  system  should  negotiate  with  the  corresponding  interference  neighbor  to  mitigate  the
interference.  For  example,  when  a  new  interfering  SS  is  found,  the  interfering  SS  should  be  allocated
resources  for  SS  operation  during  its  serving  BS’s  Master  subframe.  If  an  interference  relationship  is
released,  the  system  should  use  the  released  resource  effectively  to  improve  frequency  efficiency. As  an
example,  the  SS  that  has  released  the  interference  relation  may  operate  during  its  serving  BS’s  Slave
subframe, or a BS may borrow the subframe released by the interference neighbor.

15.1.3.2 Procedure flow for SS

The procedures for system and community entry for a new SS in WirelessMAN-CX are as follows:

— The new SS starts the network entry procedures using the UL Master subframe
— The  new  SS  listens  to  the  Medium  and  the  Coexistence  Control  Channel  (CXCC)  allocations  to

detect interference (see 15.1.4.3)

— At BS request, the new SS reports to the BS the results of the CXCC measurements
— At BS command, the new SS transmits at the appropriate allocations in the CXCC

— If a neighbor operating base station (OBS) perceives interference from the new SSs, it may ask the

new base station to find another channel/subframe for that SS operation

15.1.3.2.1 Channel measurement in the operating stage

A BS may request an SS to measure one or more channels on its behalf in the operating stage. A BS should
schedule  the  available  measurement  interval  for  SS  via  OFDMA  Periodic  Channel  Measurement  IE
(8.4.5.3.34). During a scheduled measurement interval, the BS shall not transmit MAC PDUs to that SS or
request any uplink transmission from any SSs. The BS should schedule the measurement interval properly in
such  a  way  that  there  is  no  effect  on  normal  traffic  transmission  between  the  BS  and  SS.  The  channel
measurement may be scheduled to cover the CXCC measurements.

Upon  receiving  a  measurement  requirement,  a  SS  shall  start  to  measure  the  indicated  channel  during  the
scheduled  measurement  intervals.  A  SS  shall  continue  to  measure  the  indicated  channel  during  the
scheduled measurement intervals until the measurement interval ends or the serving BS schedules the SS to
receive and/or send signals or information during the measurement interval.

A  BS  may  schedule  one or  more  measurement  patterns  for  an  SS. The  measurement  interval  of  different
measurement  patterns  shall  not  be  overlapped.  Measurement  patterns  are  identified  by  a  Measurement
Request  index  parameter  in  a  Periodic  Channel  Measurement  IE.  The  SS  should  report  its  measurement
result corresponding to each measurement request from the BS.

15.1.4 Basic and extended coordinated coexistence

15.1.4.1 Functionality for the basic and extended coordinated coexistence

The  spectrum  is  considered  to  be  constituted  from  frequency  slots  called  “frequency  channels”  and
repetitive time slots called “subframes.”

The functionality for different levels of coexistence is detailed as follows:

a)

Functionality for basic coordinated coexistence:
1) The  systems  sharing  the  spectrum  shall  synchronize  their  transmissions  by  using  a  GPS  or

equivalent absolute time indicator.

2) Every system shall have the opportunity to evaluate the maximum possible interference on a

frequency channel and on a subframe within well-known time intervals.

3) Every  operating system shall  transmit at  its  maximum  operational power within well-known

time intervals, so that other systems can measure the interference that is created.

4) Every  system shall have an  opportunity to use well-defined repetitive time intervals (Master

subframes) for operating with acceptable interference.

5) No system is allowed to create harmful interference to any SS of a system during the victim

systems’ Master subframe.

6) A  system  shall  not  become  the  Master  of  a  subframe  that  is  already  designated  as  a  Master

subframe of an interfering system.

7) All  the  systems  need  to  have  the  possibility  to  use  well-known  time  intervals  in  common
(Shared subframes), but their transmit powers need to be limited to minimize the accumulated
interference.

b)

Functionality for extended coordinated coexistence:
1)

Systems  (Slave  systems)  may  use  the  Master  subframes  owned  by  other  systems  with  the
following conditions:

Authorized licensed use limited to: John Greninger. Downloaded on April 01,2019 at 05:32:44 UTC from IEEE Xplore.  Restrictions apply.

2431

IEEE Std 802.16-2017
IEEE Standard for Air Interface for Broadband Wireless Access Systems

i)

The  operation  in  Slave  mode  may  be  provisioned  based  on  operator  agreements;  these
agreements may use power control, antenna orientation, MIMO operation, etc.

ii) The systems owning a Master subframe should identify the transmitter of a Slave system

causing interference;

iii) A Master system should communicate with a Slave system to require the reduction of the

transmitted power of those units which create interference;

iv) A Slave system shall satisfy the requests of a Master system relative to the reduction of the
transmit  power,  in  case  that  the  usage  of  Slave  subframes  is  not  coordinated  by
administrative means.

2)

Slave systems may get the Master system’s allowance for usage of their subframes for limited
time intervals. The allowance is obtained if all the Master systems using the same subframes
accept the request.

15.1.4.2 Master allocation

Within the four frames in one CX-Frame, there are three frames that may be allocated to different systems as
Master, i.e., there are up to three Master allocations in one CX-Frame. They can optimally accommodate a
number of systems in neighborhood.

15.1.4.3 Coexistence Control Channel

The Coexistence Control Channel (CXCC) is based on a periodic pattern of synchronized time slots used in
a coordinated mode and allowing the following basic functionality:

— Secondary synchronization
— Detection of specific spectrum users
— Detection of bursty spectrum users
— Evaluation of cumulated interference during Master subframes
— Intersystem communication using same-PHY profile
— Intersystem communication using DL timing adjustment for coexistence signaling

15.1.4.4 Coordinated operation for basic coexistence

The  IBS  may  be  provisioned  for  operation,  based  on  operator  coordination,  or  may  follow  the  cognitive
procedures described in 15.4. In case of provisioning, the operators may provision operational parameters as
the operating frequency channel, CX-Frame type, and Master subframe operation.

When using cognitive procedures, an IBS shall listen to the CXCC on all its operating channels and all the
available subframes. Based on this, a BS shall determine the availability of a less-interfered subframe and its
corresponding frequency channel.

The BS shall occupy the chosen subframe and shall start to operate as Master in the subframe. The system
controlled by the BS shall claim the Master frame by transmitting on the CXCC.

15.1.5 Architecture for WirelessMAN-CX

The architecture for Radio Resource Management in the context of this clause is a distributed one and allows
communication and exchange of parameters between different systems. This architecture is used in support
of the Coordinated Coexistence Protocol for interference identification, prevention, and resolution. Every
system should include a database (DB) to store the shared information regarding the actual usage and the
intended usage of the radio resource. Note that a central Network Control and Management system may also
be an element in this architecture. This entity may designate the operating frequency channels and Master
subframes.

Once a BS has learned its potential coexistence neighbor topology from the BSIS, it evaluates the coexisting
BSs  and  identifies  which  BSs  might  create  interference.  For  each  of  the  potential  coexistence  neighbors,
using the operation frequencies and bandwidth of the other systems and taking into account the net filter
discrimination,  the Adaptive  Channel  Selection  will  select  the  actual  operating  frequency,  such  that  the
probability of interference should be minimized. Each BS tries to form its own community, by including the
coexistence neighbor BSs that create interference to the associated SSs. The members of a community will
change  when  the  working  frequency  of  any  BS  changes  or  a  new  interfering  coexistence  neighbor  BS
comes in.

Within  a  BSIS,  a WirelessMAN-CX  BS  can  construct  its  coexistence  neighbor  topology  and  acquire  the
network addresses of its coexistence neighbors securely.

15.2 Provisioning for WirelessMAN-CX

In order to achieve basic coordinated coexistence, as defined in 15.1.4, the following provisions are needed
for a WirelessMAN-CX system.

15.2.1 Synchronization of WirelessMAN-CX and WirelessMAN-UCP systems

15.2.1.1 Common clock

All base stations forming a community of users sharing a common radio spectrum shall use a common clock
to synchronize their MAC frames.

Such a clock can be provided by global navigational systems such as GPS or by an IEEE 1588 [B31] or a
Network Time Protocol (NTP) server of sufficient accuracy to meet the requirements of 15.2.1.2. Every BS
shall, as a first step upon activation, ensure the derivation of the common system clock.

WirelessMAN-CX systems, which do not receive the signals of a global navigation system satellite or do not
receive the appropriate information from an IEEE 1588 [B31] or a NTP Server, may synchronize their BS
with the operating WirelessMAN-CX systems, using the information distributed by CXCC. Such systems
shall  check  their  synchronization  status  periodically,  with  a  maximum  of  10  min  elapsed  time  between
successive checks.

15.2.1.2  Network Time Interval and CX_MAC_NO Frame start

All  synchronized  WirelessMAN-CX  base  stations  shall  derive  a  1  pps  clock  broadcast  by  a  global
navigational system or other means. The 1 s duration is called the Network Time Interval (NTI). The rising
edge of the 1 pps synchronization pulse shall be considered as the start of the NTI and of the WirelessMAN-
CX MAC Frame. The 1 pps pulse shall have a stability of ±50 nanoseconds, as measured from rising edge to
rising edge.

15.2.1.3 Granularity of the NTI

The NTI is composed of 1000 NTI_S intervals. NTI_S units can be determined internally by the BS or SS,
being derived from the NTI. NTI_S units can alternatively be supplied directly to the BS or SS by the global
navigational system receivers used to determine the NTI.

15.2.1.4 UTC standard time

The  common  clock  specified  in  15.2.1  shall  provide  a  coordinated  universal  time  (UTC)  signal  to  all
WirelessMAN-CX systems, making all systems synchronized to this referenced timestamp. WirelessMAN-
CX base stations shall use the UTC time standard for coordinating and identifying specific NTI intervals.
One millisecond granularity of the UTC standard time shall be provided by specifying the NTI_S units.

15.2.1.6 Transmit/Receive synchronization

In order to achieve the co-location of different access networks, it is necessary to use the same MAC Frame
duration and the same DL/UL splitting. The default value of the Frame duration is 5 ms.

In the license-exempt regulatory domains, the DL/UL splitting in TDD operation shall be set for compliant
systems to be 60%/40%.

15.2.2 Same PHY profile

For systems using the same PHY profile in this standard, the profile elements are as follows:

— Channel width
— PHY mode option:

— WirelessMAN-OFDM (256 point FFT)
— WirelessMAN OFDMA 128, 512, 1024, or 2048 point FFT, depending on channel bandwidth

Intersystem communication is effective between systems using the same PHY profile.

15.2.3 Additional ranging requirements for WirelessMAN-CX systems

A  WirelessMAN-CX  BS  shall  only  schedule  ranging  opportunities  in  UL  subframes  for  which  it  is  the
Master or can otherwise guarantee interference-free operation relative to other WirelessMAN-CX systems.
It is the BS’s responsibility to guarantee sufficient ranging opportunities for its operational environment.

15.3 Interference assessment and basic connectivity creation

In order to coordinate with the neighbor systems, a system should be aware of its interference situation and
identify the victims and sources around it. Based on this, the systems can proceed with further interference
prevention (15.4) procedures.

CXCC is the main enabler for the interference assessment during the various Master subframes. Based on
such  assessments,  a  system  may  chose  the  least  interfered  Master  subframes  for  its  operation.  The
interference during the Master subframes may be alternatively estimated by other ways.

A WirelessMAN-CX  system  and  its  neighboring  systems  should  use  coordinated  mechanisms  to  become
aware of the identity of the interferer, when they are able to exchange information between each other. This
subclause  defines  the  identification  procedures  based  on  information  exchange  using  signaling  and
messages.

The BS in the system takes responsibility for gathering and maintaining all the interference information of
the system and determines the resources allocated for its own system use. Subscriber stations as well gather
and maintain interference information pertinent to themselves and can provide this information to their base
stations to augment the interference database for the whole system.

All the corresponding interference information should be stored in the distributed database (as SS and BS
interference tables) for each system (see Annex Q) and maintained regularly. The distributed database has
the information related to all the systems in the neighborhood or in other communities.

15.3.1 Coexistence Control Channel

The Coexistence Control Channel (CXCC) is based on a series of globally synchronized time slots, each of
duration of Tcc_s allocated at periods of Tcc (see 10.5.1) dedicated for coexistence functions. It uses about
1% of system resources.

15.3.1.1 Basic principles

The CXCC allocation usage shall follow the following rules:

— The CXCC allocations are mapped to Master and Shared subframes.
— During the CXCC Master allocations, no Slave or Shared activity is allowed; however, depending
on context, the Master subframes may be used for transmitting regular data. The optional common
subframe shall not be transmitted.

— The timing of the CXCC allocation, relative to the MAC Frame, is given in 10.5.1.
— The timing of the CSI allocation is given in 10.5.2.
— CX_MAC  Frame  numbering  is  binary  having  the  length  of  10  bits;  the  CX_MAC_NO  =  0  is
synchronized with the absolute time 00:00:00 UTC. CX_MAC_NO is incremented by 1 every MAC
Frame.

— The  repetition  period  of  CXCC  (Tcxcc,  see  10.5.1)  for  5 ms  MAC  Frames  is  5.12 s  (1024  MAC
Frames). Four CXCC cycles constitute a CXCC Multi-Frame. The current value of the MAC Frame
is  provided  by  the  12-bit  CXCC-Frame-NO  and  is  transmitted  as  a  TLV  of  the  DCD  message.
CXCC-Frame-NO = 0 is synchronized with CX_MAC_NO = 0.

— Based  on  the  current  value  of  the  CXCC-Frame-NO,  all  the  system  components  (BS,  SS,  etc.)

should implement the CXCC functionality suitable to the current CXCC frame.

— A  CXCC  subchannel  is  formed  from  eight  CXCC  allocations,  mapped  within  Master  and  Shared

subframes, four for the DL and four for the UL.

— The CXCC four subchannels are scheduled in consecutive order.

— The duration of a CXCC subchannel is as follows:
— 1024/4 = 256 MAC frames (1280 ms)
— The CXCC allocations appear in average every 256/4 = 64 MAC Frames (320 ms).

— The CXCC allocations during any one of CXCC subchannel 1–4 are as follows:

— Master allocation 1: CX_MAC_NO mod 256 = 0
— Master allocation 2: CX_MAC_NO mod 256 = 64 + 1
— Master allocation 3: CX_MAC_NO mod 256 = 128 + 2
— Shared allocation: CX_MAC_NO mod 256 = 192 + 3
— The CXCC allocations during CSI subchannel is as follows:

— OCSI for the system with Master allocation 1: CX_MAC_NO mod 4 = 0
— OCSI for the system with Master allocation 2: CX_MAC_NO mod 4 = 1
— OCSI for the system with Master allocation 3: CX_MAC_NO mod 4 = 2
— ICSI for the initialization system: CX_MAC_NO mod 4 = 3

15.3.1.2.1 Subchannel 1

Subchannel  1  is  composed  by  intervals  during  which  the  IEEE  802.16  systems  shall  remain  quiet.  This
silence interval will allow the identification of SSUs, operating in a specific frequency band.

The CXCC subchannel 1 uses the defined MAC Frames within the CX MAC Frame numbers 0–255.

15.3.1.2.2 Subchannel 2

Subchannel  2  should  be  used  for  the  transmission  of  interference  identification  messages  and  subframe
claiming  processes  between  systems  using  a  same  PHY  profile,  which  is  specified  as  PUSC,  5 MHz
channel,  512  FFT  size  and  using  the  permutation  base  equal  with  zero. A  system  claims  a  subframe  by
continually  occupying  a  specific  Master  subframe  in  the  downlink  and  uplink.  This  is  accomplished  by
sending BSD and SSURF messages every subchannel 2 repetition period. Such transmissions (messages in
CMI) should be undertaken only by the system claiming a specific CXCC allocation, while all other systems
shall remain silent.

The  DL  CMI  are  identified  as  CX_CMI_D(n)  for  messages  sent  on  the  (n = 1– 3)  Master  subframes  of
subchannel  2.  Master  subframes  are  claimed  and  continually  used  by  the  claiming  WirelessMAN-CX
system to indicate its operation and use of the channel and its associated subframes.

For n = 4, the CMI is sent on the Shared subframe, and only on an occasional basis by a system (this is used
for identification of sporadic interference emanating from outside the coexistence community).

The complement of the downlink CMI are the uplink intervals, identified as CX_CMI_U(n).

BSD messages shall be sent in the downlink CMI and SSURF messages shall be sent on the uplink.

The  CXCC  subchannel  2,  containing  the  CMI,  shall  use  the  defined  MAC  Frames  within  the  CX  MAC
Frame numbers 256–511.

CMI operation is described in 15.3.3.

15.3.1.2.3 Subchannel 3

Subchannel 3 shall be used for the Primary synchronization and for detection of non-SSUs.

The CXCC subchannel 3 shall use the defined MAC Frames within the CX MAC Frame numbers 512–767.
Subchannel 3 shall expand over the CXCC Multi-Frame, as follows:

— Cycle 1: Primary sync
— Cycle 2: Detection of non-SSU
— Cycle 3: Detection of non-SSU
— Cycle 4: Detection of non-SSU

During the cycles 2, 3, and 4, the WirelessMAN-CX and WirelessMAN-UCP systems shall be silent.

In  Cycle  1(primary  sync),  only  the  BSs  using  GPS  or  equivalent  synchronization  shall  transmit.  The
preambles at the DL subframe start should be used as the primary synchronization signals.

15.3.1.2.4 Subchannel 4

Interference  assessment  of  WirelessMAN-CX  compliant  systems  is  performed  during  subchannel  4.  A
WirelessMAN-CX compliant system shall always transmit during subchannel 4 of its Master subframes.

The data transmitted during subchannel 4 shall use the operational channel width and permutations.

The  data  or  Interference  Evaluation  Bursts  shall  be  transmitted  using  the  maximum  operational  power
during the corresponding Master subframes. If regular data transmission is used, it should be scheduled in
such a way to represent the power density characteristics of cumulated Interference Evaluation Bursts.

The  message  CX-FWD-REQ  with  action  code:  BSD  or  action  code:  SSURF,  containing  only  TLVs
providing the location information of the BS and fixed SS, should be transmitted in the first CXCC cycle of
the CXCC multi-frame, using the system’s Master subframe. The scheduling information for transmitting
SSURF is provided by the CX-UL-MAP transmitted in the Master frame of the previous CX-Frame.

The  location  information  shall  not  be  transmitted  in  case  that  the  local  regulations  or  policies  forbid  the
dissemination of this information.

Every  system  using  a  specific  Master  subframe  shall  use  the  CXCC  allocation  mapped  into  that  Master
subframe  for  letting  a  new  system  to  assess  the  maximum  interference  within  that  Master  subframe  and
frequency  channel.  The  operation  of  a  system  during  its  Slave  subframes  and  Shared  subframes  is  not
allowed.

CXCC subchannel 4 uses the operational channel size, FFT size and subcarrier permutation. It is mapped
within the CX MAC Frame numbers 768–1023.

15.3.1.2.5 CSI subchannel

The CSI (see 15.3.4.1) shall be allocated, if supported, according to the CSI duration (10.5.2) of each DL
subframe within CX-Frame.

The  CSI  subchannel  is  used  for  interference  identification  and  basic  connectivity  creation  within
interference neighborhood. ICSI shall be allocated within the shared frame, which is used for the initializing
of  WirelessMAN-CX  systems.  OCSI  shall  be  allocated  for  each  WirelessMAN-CX  system  within  the
Master allocation used for the operation of that system.

The CSI sequence shall skip the usage of time intervals within the frame allocated for CXCC subchannel 1.

The detailed structure is presented in 15.3.4.1.

The CSI allocations and operation are described in 15.3.4.

15.3.1.3 Operation of other WirelessMAN system variants during the CXCC

Other  variants  of  WirelessMAN  systems  operating  in  the  same  geographic  region  and  spectrum  as  a
WirelessMAN-CX system shall be silent during the time intervals allocated for the operation of the CXCC
subchannels 1–3. Note that this requires the capability to synchronize sufficiently (see 15.2.1) to determine
which frames constitute the CXCC.

15.3.2 Candidate Channel and Master Frame Assessment (CCMFA)

Candidate  Channel  and  Master  Frame  Assessment  (CCMFA)  is  a  process  used  by  WirelessMAN-CX
systems  in  a  given  frequency  range,  to  evaluate  the  radio  environment  within  each  candidate  frequency
channel.  The  BS  monitors  the  candidate  channels  and  subframes  in  CX-Frame  within  a  band,  to  find  a
frequency  channel  and  Master  subframes  that  provide  the  highest  capacity  and/or  least  amount  of
interference. This process is used, for example, by an IBS prior to forming a coexistence community.

2439

IEEE Std 802.16-2017
IEEE Standard for Air Interface for Broadband Wireless Access Systems

The CCMFA utilizes passive scanning to determine if the IBS is a potential interference victim and active
scanning to determine if the IBS is a potential interference source. Passive scanning involves monitoring
uplink transmission intervals and measurement of wireless medium by measuring the potential interference
signal power [I]. Active scanning involves broadcasting a signal that advertises the presence of the IBS, so
that a potential interference victim operating system that supports this feature can measure the interference
created and potentially contact the IBS neighbor for further collaboration.

The  CXCC  subchannel  4  (15.3.1.2.4)  offers  a  method  for  the  IBS  to  determine  its  susceptibility  as  an
interference  victim  by  measuring  the  level  of  interference  during  each  potential  Master  subframe  using
passive scanning. Alternatively, SSURF provides for a method of passive scanning by monitoring messages
in UL subframes within CXCC subchannel 2, while the CXCC CSI subchannel provides a method of active
scanning  using  signal  broadcasting. Also,  it  is  possible  for  the  BSIS  to  be  used  to  calculate  the  expected
interference in the BS area.

In passive scanning, each candidate channel and Master subframe shall be ranked in terms of interference-
to-noise ratio (INR). Those channels and Master subframes with the lowest INR shall be marked as available
by  the base  station. They  will  therefore  become candidates  for  entry  by  an  IBS, since such  channels  and
Master subframes have the lowest amount of discernible activity on them, which implies that they are likely
to have lower interference.

In  active  scanning,  the  BS  should  broadcast  its  identification  and  relative  information  using  signaling/
messaging  within  each  available  channel.  All  of  the  SSs  in  potential  interference  victim  systems  can
measure the impact of interference from the IBS over their specific CXCC allocation, and store the ID of the
IBS  and  the  relative  information  (see  15.3.4.2  and  15.3.3.3)  in  the  interference  database.  By  receiving  a
report  from  the  victim  SSs,  the  OBS  in  the  victim  system  can  have  an  entire  view  of  the  interference
environment  of  each  SS  within  its  system  and  can  contact  the  interference  source  IBS  for  further
interference control (15.4).

Channels should be further ranked according to the number of available Master subframes. A higher number
of available Master subframes indicates a less crowded channel.

15.3.3 CXCC subchannel 2

This subchannel is used for coexistence messaging mechanisms.

Interference  resolution  amongst  systems  having  the  same  profile  is  undertaken  by  the  transmission,
reception, and detection of messages sent during coexistence messaging intervals (CMI). A WirelessMAN-
CX system using CMI as an interference control technique has scheduled intervals on the CXCC subchannel
2 (see 15.3.1.2.2) to transmit identity data unique to itself during the CMI claimed by the system. All other
WirelessMAN-CX  systems,  by  detecting  and  decoding  these  messages,  can  determine  the  origin  of  the
interference, determine the radiation characteristics of the interference emitter, and can quantify the severity
of  its  effects.  Such  messaging  implements  interference  sensing  and  identification  required  for  cognitive
radio applications. WirelessMAN-CX systems can use sensed information to alter their temporal or spatial
emission  characteristics  in  support  of  coexistence  with  other  similar  systems  or  avoid  or  accommodate
interference caused by other non-WirelessMAN-CX systems.

15.3.3.1 Coexistence messaging interval

The location of a specific CMI is defined by its UL/DL CX_MAC_NO, which is referenced with respect to
a universally synchronized time source. There are four CMI, each with a DL and UL slot in the CXCC Tcxcc
cycle. The slots are labeled CX_CMI_Dn and CX_CMI_Un where (n = 1– 4).

CMIs are used by WirelessMAN-CX systems (BSs and their SSs) to mediate their co-channel coexistence.
The CMI provide an opportunity for systems to indicate to each other the extent of the interference they can

cause;  newly  arriving  IBSs  shall  use  the  CMI  to  make  themselves  known  to  established  communities  of
operating base stations (OBS). Newly entering SS make their presence known when they are detected by
base stations to which they are not associated.

Each system claims a unique CMI by a process outlined in 15.3.3.3. A system shall broadcast its BSD and
SSURF messages (which are CX-FWD messages with Action Codes BSD and SSURF respectively) in its
claimed  downlink  and  uplink  CMI;  when  it  does  this  all  other  members  of  the  coexistence  community
remain  silent  and  monitor  to  detect  the  extent  of  the  interference  that  is  caused  by  these  specific
transmissions.

Figure 15-6  gives  a  schematic  temporal  representation  of  how  the  BSD  and  SSURF  messages  are  used
within  the  CXCC  to  claim  subframes  or  indicate  their  availability.  Within  OFDMA-based  systems,
consideration shall also be given to the use of specific subchannelizations known to the WirelessMAN-CX
system in order for the Coexistence Messaging Mechanism concept to work. SSURF messages are sent on
specific known subchannels and subcarrier permutation (see 15.3.3.5).

15.3.3.2 Interference identification using Coexistence Messaging Mechanisms

The BSD message uniquely identifies the base station controlling the system with which a particular CMI is
associated. SSURF messages are unique to the subscriber stations associated with the same base station and
associated with the same CMI.

Every  BSD  (see  15.3.3.4)  sent  downlink  has  a  BSID  associated  with  it.  The  BSID,  when  received  by  a
foreign SS, indicates the source of interference to the foreign SS. The SSURF messages (see 15.3.3.5) when
received by a foreign BS, indicate to the foreign BS the sources of interference to it. Only one BSD message
is inserted into the downlink CMI; whereas, multiple SSURFs are scheduled and inserted inside the uplink
CMI (15.3.3.1).

CMI  slots  CX_CMI_D/U  (1–3)  are  used  exclusively for  claiming  subframes  and  interference  messaging.
These  slots  are  associated  with  the  three  Master  subframes  of  the  CXCC  repetitive  cycle.  CMI  slot
CX_CMI_D/U(4) is used for identification of sporadic users and is associated with the Shared subframe of
the CXCC cycle subchannel 2.

Normally the CMI claiming process and the Candidate Channel and Master Frame Assessment (15.3.2), that
every BS undertakes before entry into the coexistence community, limits a single system to a unique CMI
and  a  specific  subframe.  However,  the  uniqueness  of  the  CMI  cannot  be  guaranteed  because  of  sporadic
interference and situations where hidden systems become visible to each other. Such situations will lead to
collisions  of  BSD  and  SSURF  messages,  making  it  difficult  to  resolve  the  sources  of  interference.  To
overcome  the  collision  processes  and  loss  of  CMI  uniqueness  in  resolving  interference,  several  other
detection processes are implemented, as described below.

All systems have access to the shared CMI subframes of the CXCC cycle, called CX_CMI_D/U(4). Every
system,  after  having  claimed  one  of  the  Master  CMI  subframes  CX_CMI_D/U(1-3)  shall  randomly  send
BSD and SSURF messages on the shared CMI subframe, once in ten CMI subframes. If the system is not
sending, then it shall remain silent over the duration of the Shared subframe, having its BS and SS operate in
the  respective  receive  states.  In  this  manner  it  is  expected  that  co-channel,  same  CMI  systems  will  have
occasional  instances  where  their  mutual  interference  detection  can  be  realized.  Once  this  is  done,  other
techniques, based on the Coexistence Protocol, will have to be implemented to reduce interference between
these systems

The  second  technique  for  identification  of  same  Master  CMI  subframe  systems  is  achieved  by  sparsely
populating  the  uplink  CMI  with  SSURF  messages.  Sparse  population  and  random  placement  of  SSURF
within  the  Tcc_s  duration  of  the  CMI  slot  ensures  that  SSURFs  from  distant  systems  have  access  to  the
detection interval offered by the shared CMI.

15.3.3.3 Community entry for systems using a common PHY profile

In applications, which are used with systems having a common (same) PHY profile, entry of a new base
station (the IBS) shall be undertaken in the following four steps, with the IBS:

— Monitoring the CX_CMI_Un uplink intervals
— Selecting an empty CX_CMI_Dn downlink interval
— Claiming an empty CX_CMI_Dn downlink interval
— Becoming a member of a coexistence community using the claimed CMI

Prior  to  entry  into  a  community  of  operating  base  stations  (OBS)  it  is  assumed  that  the  IBS  will  have
undertaken the Candidate Channel and Master Frame Assessment (15.3.2) process, has selected a candidate
channel  and  has  no  operational  SS  yet  deployed.  The  IBS  shall  be  synchronized  to  the  universal  timing
standard  and  can  determine  the  position  of  the  CXCC  subchannel  2  CMI.  It  is  assumed  that  the  IBS  is
deployed within an interference neighborhood, e.g., active interference from existing operating systems is
present. The IBS entry process is shown in Figure 15-7.

a) Monitoring the CX_CMI_Un uplink intervals

b)

Having tuned to the candidate channel, the IBS shall monitor and determine the level of activity on
each  uplink  interval  CX_CMI_Un  (n = 1 – 3)  by  demodulating  the  uplink  SSURF  (see  15.3.3.5)
messages  and  storing  their  parameters  in  its  Base  Station  Information. All  demodulated  SSURF
messages will be from SSs that will interfere with the BS on the uplink. Eventually, coexistence will
have to be negotiated with each of the OBS controlling these SSs. Each CMI from CX_CMI_U1 to
CX_CMI_U3 is monitored. Each interval shall be monitored over the duration of 10 Tcxcc cycles.
Additionally, during this time the CXCC subchannel 1 Silent Intervals shall be monitored as well
and  if  there  is  detectable  power  on  them  (i.e.,  when  ((N + I)/N) > 1  dB),  the  channel  shall
be construed  as  occupied  by  a  non-WirelessMAN-CX  systems.  The  channel  shall  then  be
abandoned, and a new candidate channel shall be tested. The flowchart for this operation is shown in
Figure 15-7.
Selecting an empty CX_CMI_Dn downlink interval
The  monitored  CX_CMI_Un  uplink  intervals  in  which  no  (demodulated)  SSURF  messages  are
received  indicate  candidate  CMI.  Empty  intervals  indicate  that  it  may  be  possible  for  the  IBS  to
form  a  coexistence  community.  (Full  loading  is  indicated  by  having  all  three  CX_CMI_D/U
intervals occupied.) Each candidate CX_CM_Un shall have a RSSI measurement undertaken on it
(see  8.4.11.2).  This  is  done  specifically  to  detect  the  presence  of  SSURF  messages  that  may  be
below  the  level  needed  for  demodulation.  Such  SSURFs,  if  they  exist,  indicate  that  the  chosen
interval  has  interference  and  that  coexistence  community  subframes  are  likely  being  used.  Each
candidate  interval  shall  be  monitored  in  this  manner  over  the  duration  of  10  Tcxcc  cycles. An
interval  shall  be  considered  as  usable  and  chosen  if  the  RSSI  measurement  results  in  a  ((N + I)/
N) < 1 dB.
The absence of uplink SSURFs means that the CX_CMI_Un is free of uplink occupancy (and likely
the  complementary  CX_CMI_Dn  is  the  same);  hence,  it  can  be  considered  as  being  ready  for
claiming.

Claiming procedure
The purpose of the claiming process is to make adjacent OBS networks (which are likely members
of different coexistence communities) aware of the presence of the IBS. Claiming is undertaken by
having the IBS broadcast its BSD during an empty CX_CMI_Dn. Since the OBS are silent and are
monitoring the downlink on each CX_CMI_Dn other than their own, the broadcast message will be
detectable during what was previously an empty interval.
To begin the claiming procedure the IBS should broadcast at maximum operational EIRP its BSD
(see 15.3.3.4) message. This message, when received by foreign SSs belonging to adjacent networks
that form the interference neighborhood, will result in those SSs informing their home base stations
(the OBS) of the presence of a new base station (the IBS) using the MAC message CX-CCID-IND
(see  6.3.2.3.86).  All  OBS  having  SSs  that  detect  the  BSD  during  the  claimed  CX_CMI_Dn
downlink interval shall, via the backhaul link, respond back to the IBS using C-CX-REQ primitives
with Action_Type=CMI_Interference_Resolution  (15.6.1.5)  informing  it  that  it  has  been  detected

d)

and is a defacto interferer on the downlink. The IBS should include in its BS information table the
network addresses of all of the OBS that have directed C-CX-REQ primitives to the IBS. The IBS
shall  continue  its  BSD  broadcast  routine  until  no  new  C-CX-REQ  with  Action_Type=CMI
Interference Resolution primitives are detected. With the receipt of the totality of primitives, the IBS
will have determined the extent of its interference neighborhood. Having this information the IBS
will  know  with  which  OBS  it  shall  negotiate  coexistence,  if  indeed  it  is  warranted.  If  it  is  not
warranted  (for  instance,  because  the  interference  created  is  too  difficult  to  resolve  by  the
Coexistence Protocol), the IBS abandons the CX_CMI_Dn and chooses an alternative channel that
is identified as part of the CCMFA process (15.3.2).
Capacity negotiation and membership in the coexistence community
The  OBS  networks  which  the  IBS  creates  or  sustains  interference  to/from  are  listed  in  the  BS
Information table of the IBS. This table contains the BSIDs and network addresses derived either
from  uplink  SSURF  messages  that  the  IBS  demodulated  during  its  monitoring  phase  or  from  the
primitives that it received via the backhaul from the OBS as part of the claiming procedure [item c)
above].
Communication and negotiation with each OBS listed in the BS Information Table is undertaken via
the Coexistence Protocol (CXP). Coexistence entails allocation of uplink and downlink transmission
intervals  in  a  manner  that  eliminates  co-channel  interference  amongst  users  that  would  otherwise
experience  it  and  sustain  degraded  communications.  This  should  be  done  by  parsing  uplink  and
downlink intervals and establishing Shared, Master, and Slave subframes (see 15.4.1.2). Each OBS
that the IBS has listed in its BS Information Table as an interfering network shall partake in such
resolution  of  interference  by  scheduling.  By  undertaking  this  process  the  IBS  thus  creates  a
coexistence  community  for  itself,  and  consequently  becomes  accommodated  by  the  neighboring
networks of its interference neighborhood.

15.3.3.4 Base Station Descriptor (BSD) message

The Base Station Descriptor (BSD) message is used for basic interference identification and establishment
of  connectivity  in  WirelessMAN-CX  systems.  This  message  is  sent  by  the  BS  only  within  a  specific
downlink  slot  CX_CMI_D(n)  in  the  CXCC  subchannel  2. Throughout  this  document  the  term  “BSD”  or
“BSD message” refers specifically to the CX-FWD-REQ coexistence message having Action Code BSD.

The  BSD  shall  be  sent  using  QPSK  1/2. This  delimits  the  furthest  radiation  extent  of  signals  capable  of
being demodulated from the base station and in essence delimits the range of interference that base station
can  cause. The  BSD  contains  information  on  the  network  address  of  the  base  station.  When  the  BSD  is
received  by  a  subscriber  station  as  interference,  the  subscriber  station  should  forward  the  information
contained  into  the  BSD  message  to  its  base  station  using  the  CX-CCID-IND  message  (6.3.2.3.86).  The
extracted  network address  can then be used  to  undertake  the  coexistence resolution  protocol between  the
source and the affected base stations.

The BSD also contains information about the EIRP, direction and type of radiation pattern, GPS location of
the base station sending the BSD, and information about the power spectral density of the whole band in
which the BSD operates. Combined with the received signal strength at the affected SS, this information is
useful  to  the  systems  affected  by  the  interference  because  it  allows  them  to  undertake  profiling  of  the
interferer’s propagation channel as seen by the affected SS. Cognitive radio algorithms controlling adaptive
antennas can be used to minimize the interference, for example, without invoking the coexistence protocols
using such information.

The  incidence  of  received  BSD  messages  from  a  specific  base  station  can  be  used  as  a  measure  of  the
interference  intensity,  indicating  to  the  affected  system  whether  coexistence  action  should  be  taken.  The
number of BSD detection events per Tcxcc cycle allows such counts. Sporadic interference can be identified
by  such  means.  The  detection  threshold  of  such  interference  can  be  set  with  CX-CCID-RES  messages
(6.3.2.3.87).

15.3.3.5 Subscriber Station Uplink Radio Frequency (SSURF) message

Throughout  this  document  the  term  “SSURF”  or  “SSURF  message”  refers  specifically  to  the  CX-FWD-
REQ coexistence message having Action Code SSURF. These messages are the primary means by which a
system defines the extent of the interference caused by its subscriber stations to neighboring base stations
and coexistence community members. It is demodulated and effectively sensed by the affected base stations.
The message is sent on a periodic basis in the CX_CMI_U(1-3) when requested to by the base station and
the transmissions can be maintained over a number of Tcxcc cycles, depending on the number of SS the BS
controls. All  of  the  SS  shall  have  an  opportunity  to  transmit  SSURF  messages  in  order  to  facilitate  their
detection  as  interference  by  other  systems.  When  received  as  interference  at  foreign  base  stations,  the
demodulated  SSURF  provides  that  station  with  its  specific  identity  and  the  network  address  of  the  BS
controlling it.

The monitoring  process  for  foreign interfering  SSURF  messages  is undertaken  by the base  station. A BS
(system n) shall monitor all CX_CMI_U(N), (N=1..4), including its own CMI, in order to identify foreign
SSURF  from  co-channel  systems  that  have  either  claimed  the  other  slots,  or  even  the  same  slot  (N = n).
Under  most  circumstances  this  should  not  occur  since  the  IBS  undergoes  an  extensive  CMI  claiming
procedure  (15.3.3.3);  however,  there  is  always  the  possibility  of  sporadic  interference  which  should  be
identified. To  facilitate such detection  the  scheduling  of uplink  SSURFs  by  the controlling BS  should  be
such that the CX_CMI_U(n) slot is never fully occupied with its own SSURF messages in order to allow the
opportunity  for  other  foreign  SSURFs  to  be  detected  without  collision  (see  15.3.3.1  and  Figure 15-6).
SSURFs  can  also  be  sent  on  an  occasional  basis  in  the  Shared  subframe  CX_CMI_U(4)  of  the  CXCC
subchannel 2.

The SSURF message also contains the EIRP at which it was sent. This is done to allow foreign BS to apply
propagation  channel  estimation  algorithms  and  other  techniques  which  may  be  able  to  resolve  specific
interference without resorting to the CXP.

To  send  a  SSURF  message  by  a  SS,  the  SS  is  granted  an  allocation  in  a  UL  subframe  corresponding  to
subchannel 2 of the coexistence channel, where the allocation start time in UL-MAP will be the start of the
uplink subframe. These uplink grants for sending SSURF are unicast to the SS. The SS sends the SSURF by
using this grant in an uplink CXCC subchannel 2 frame. A long preamble is added to the SSURF message
(for OFDM operation). Additionally, the preamble preceding to the SSURF also uses a predefined CP.

CX_CMI_U consists of the last 18 OFDMA symbols in a 5ms frame. Every 12 uplink slots are defined as a
SSURF  transmission  opportunity  in  CX_CMI_U  zone.  Since  there  are  3  OFDMA  symbols  in  each  slot,
every  CX_CMI_U  zone  contains  8  SSURF  transmission  opportunities.  The  remainder  6  uplink  slots,
appearing  in  subchannel  16  of  the  CX_CMI_U,  are  reserved  and  are  not  mapped.  The  first  SSURF
transmission  opportunity  in  CX_CMI_U  starts  at  the  lowest  subchannel  and  lowest  OFDMA  slot  in  the
CX_CMI_U  zone. The  SSURF  transmission  opportunity  is  sequentially  mapped  onto  all  of  the  OFDMA
symbol indices at that subchannel assignment. When the edge of the UL zone is reached, the transmission
opportunity wraps around to the next subchannel assignment and, starting from the lowest number OFDMA
symbol, continues for all the OFDMA symbol indices at that subchannel assignment. Figure 15-8 shows the
SSURF transmission opportunity allocation map.

During every SSURF transmission opportunity, 576 bits can be transmitted. The unused bits are reserved to
be used in the future.

The  SSURF  transmission  opportunity  IE  in  the  CX-UL-MAP  is  used  to  signal  the  SSURF  transmission
opportunity assigned to each SS. The SS will send its SSURF messages during this assignment.

15.3.4 Coexistence signaling mechanisms

The coexistence signalling mechanisms are defined in order to provide the basic connectivity information
between neighbor systems which may be using different PHY profiles.

15.3.4.1 Coexistence Signaling Interval

The  Coexistence  Signaling  Interval  (CSI)  is  a  predefined  reserved  short  time  slot  at  the  end  of  a  DL
subframe, in which only one BS may transmit data. The BS uses CSI to identify itself to its neighbor systems
through one or more SSs in its neighbor system, which have received the signaling at a level higher than the
acceptable  interference  threshold  (see  Figure 15-9).  The  timing  of  each  system  within  the  neighborhood
shall be synchronized, by using a unique time reference in the same region such as GPS (or equivalent), or
by using synchronization mechanism in adhoc manner such as CXCC subchannel 1 or subchannel 3. Every
CSI shall be assigned to specific BS in a neighborhood. For the Initializing BS (IBS), the correspondent CSI
is called the ICSI (Initialization Coexistence Signaling Interval) which is allocated in the shared frame in
CX-Frame. ICSI is used by the IBS to contact its neighbor Operating BSs (OBSs). By coordination with the
other BSs, the IBS may get its Operation Coexistence Signaling Interval (OCSI ), which is allocated into one
of the three Master frame allocation in CX-Frame. Once a BS have started the operating stage and claimed
its Master frame, this BS should occupy the OCSI within this Master frame, and release the ICSI for IBS
(see, e.g., Figure 15-10).

CSI slots shall be located before  the TTG in the TTD frame  structure  (see e.g.,  Figure 15-9). The timing
parameter and the allocation of CSI may be broadcast in DCD (see 11.4.1) in the WirelessMAN-CX system
by the BS.

An example of the timing indication is illustrated in Figure 15-10. The first IBS that enters an environment
where none of the OCSIs is occupied uses the ICSI to broadcast coexistence signaling. Then, since it has not
detected any other CSI signal, it becomes OBS1 and chooses OCSI1 as the OCSI occupied for its system.
Afterwards IBS2 starts up and uses ICSI to broadcast coexistence signaling. It finds its neighbor system,
OBS1, occupying OCSI1, chooses OCSI2 as its OCSI and become OBS2 after the initializing phase (see
also 15.3.4.1.2). IBS2 can be made aware of the occupation of OCSI1 by OBS1 either by detecting signal
from  the  system  OBS1,  or  by  information  received  via  CXP  messages  as  feedback  to  the  IBS2’s
broadcasting signals by the OBS1’s SSs.

15.3.4.1.1 DL timing adjustment for coexistence signaling

The  information  carried  in  the  CSI  slots  shall  be  broadcast  by  the  BS  and  received  by  the  SSs  in  a
coexistence neighbor system. The PHY technology of the interference source system may be different from
the PHY technology of the interference victim system.

The information unit in the CSI slot is bit, carried by the timing of transmission in CSI. The duration of the
CSI length is counted by symbols according to the technology that the system is using. The CSI shall be
located right before the TTG gap, and at the end of the last downlink burst send by the BS. The BS shall set
the transmission timing parameter (see 10.5.2) according to the bit value that it is sending. The SS in the
victim system monitors the signal strength in CSI duration to get each bit value within the CSI sequence (see
15.3.4.1.3).

If a BS transmits normal data during the CSI slot, it shall mean a logical “1” to the SSs in other systems. If
the BS does not transmit data during the CSI slot, it shall mean a logical “0” to the SSs in other systems. The
timing of the CSI slot is described in 10.5.2. The timing is shown in Figure 15-11.

15.3.4.1.2 CSI scheduling

CSI is used by the BSs to broadcast signaling to the neighbor systems (see 15.3.4.1). Such signaling is used
for  interference  identification.  In  order  to  prevent  collision  with  the  other  neighboring  interferers,  the
coordinated community should prevent neighboring systems from using the same CSI allocation. There is
one ICSI for IBS and three OCSIs for three OBSs within a CX-Frame. Thus, there can be no more than three
systems neighboring with each other according to the capacity limitation of the CX-Frame. In its working
channel, each SS in the system can keep monitoring three OCSIs, one of them occupied by its serving BS;
the other two can be respectively occupied by two neighbor systems that may cause harmful interference to
this SS. In case two systems in the neighborhood are using the same Master subframe, and a SS receives
signal  from  both  in  the  same  OCSI  allocation,  the  system  may  use  the  collision  detection  and  resolution
procedure described in 15.3.4.4.

In the initialization phase of a BS, before the BS has an OCSI allocation, the BS should use ICSI to advertise
itself at each candidate channel sequentially one by one until it finds a proper channel. The neighbor OBS
should  then  send  their  current  OCSI  allocation  and  current  subframe  allocation  to  the  IBS  using  CXP
message. After  the  IBS  chooses  the  working  channel  for  its  radio  link,  the  IBS  shall  choose  a  vacant
subframe  as  its  Master,  thus  the  OCSI  within  this  Master  subframe  in  the  CX-Frame  in  this  channel  is
chosen accordingly. Then it shall inform other neighbors about this information. Then, this BS should start
using this OCSI allocation as its exclusive CSI allocation.

See Figure 15-12 for an example of the OCSI scheduling in a simple coexisted community. A system may
passive and active scan (15.3.2) all the potential working channel and record all the neighboring system’s
OCSI  allocation  in  its  coexistence  information  database  (Annex Q).  For  the  reason  of  the  CX-Frame
structure, an occupied OCSI in the record also indicates that the corresponding Master subframe has been
claimed by the occupier of the OCSI. By inquiring these records, a system may verify a suitable channel and
Master  subframe  and  the  corresponding  radio  resource  allocation  or  optimization  scheme  for  operation
(15.4), either in its initialization phase or in the operation phase.

A system experiencing harmful interference on a channel that cannot be coordinated with the interference
source is a channel that is not able to perform collaborative mechanisms.

The initializing BS uses the OCSI allocation table to find out its neighbors in the working channel. Using the
contact information it acquired from the CXP messages, the IBS may use CXP messages to negotiate for
interference resolution with its neighbors (see 15.4).

15.3.4.1.3 CSI sequence structure

The CSI sequence is broadcast from the base station to the coexistence neighbor’s subscriber station, within
a series of CSI slots fragmentally. The CSI sequence consists of a bit carried in each CSI slot as the basic
element and carries the information from the BS to the coexistence neighbor’s SS. The CSI sequence shall
start  at  the  first  CX-Frame  in  the  CXCC  cycle  in  each  system  that  was  synchronized  within  the
neighborhood. CSI sequences have a fixed length of 256 bits, where the bits left after the payload and CRC
shall always be padded by zero. The CSI sequence shall always start with 8 bits one (start-of-sequence), and
end with 8 bits zero (end-of-sequence). Each CSI sequence shall have 8 bits cyclic redundancy check (CRC)
(Polynomial “X8 + X2 + X + 1”) appended to check the validity of the information carried within the CSI

structure was detected.

15.3.4.2 Community entry of new BS using CSI

To  enter  the  existing  community  at  its  neighborhood,  a  new  BS—the  IBS—without  any  associated  SS
contacts its neighbors using the network. The new BS should synchronize to the timing of the CSI and ICSI
in the air before using ICSI to broadcast the BS Neighborhood Update Request BroadCasting (BS_NURBC)
(see  15.3.4.3)  signaling  or  BSD  messaging  to  make  its  neighbors  know  of  its  operation  and  its  contact
information.  BS_NURBC  signaling  message  includes  a  random  temporary  key  (RTK),  the  BSID  and  the
network address, while BSD messaging message includes BSID, network address and other information.

ICSI is used by the IBS to create basic connectivity with its neighbor BSs. The IBS shall use the ICSI slot to
broadcast its network address and its BSID to its neighborhood. When the SSs in the neighboring system
receives  the  signaling  broadcast  from  the  IBS,  it  shall  forward  the  information  to  its  serving  BS,  a
coexistence neighbor operating BS (OBS). So that the OBS can contact the IBS neighbor via the network. In
order to identify the coexistence request from an unauthenticated internet terminal (such as a terminal far
away or some terminal without any capability of WirelessMAN-CX air signaling, but has known the static
BSID and network address information by other method, a RTK should be used in the broadcast signaling.
To authenticate the request of a CXP message, the RTK sender requires the feedback to contain this random
temporary key.

After the basic connectivity built up, the IBS and OBS can begin further negotiations via their network using
the  coexistence  protocol.  After  coordination  with  the  neighbors  in  the  community,  the  IBS  may  get  a
periodic interference-free OCSI. Becoming an OBS, the IBS shall stop occupying the ICSI.

The  BS_NURBC  (see  15.3.4.3)  procedure  is  unidirectional,  only  from  the  BS  to  the  SSs  in  the  common
coverage area of the BS and its neighbors, and the SSs shall report all the useful information to the OBSs
they are associated with. The SSs that succeed in receiving the BS_NURBC message shall report the content
of  the  message  using  REP-RSP  (see  6.3.2.3.33)  or  CX-CSI-MNTR-REP  (6.3.2.3.95),  together  with  the
frame  number  of  the  starting  sequence  of  BS_NURBC  to  the  BS.  The  SSs  that  have  received  the  BSD
message shall report the content of the message using CX-CCID-IND (6.3.2.3.86) to the BS. The IBS uses
ICSI to broadcast the BS_NURBC or BSD message, the content of the message will enable its neighboring
systems to communicate with the IBS over the network and coordinate their operation by the coexistence
protocol.

The SSs that fail to receive the BS_NURBC, but still identify it as interference in the CSI shall report a REP-
RSP or CX-CSI-MNTR-REP message containing the error status and the starting frame number of receiving
the interference in the CSI. Using the address of the IBS’s network and the BSID reported by the SSs that
have successfully decoded the BS_NURBC message, together with the RTK, the OBSs communicate with
the  IBS  over  the  network  via  their  network.  By  checking  the  frame  number  in  the  report,  the  OBS
determines  if  the  SSs  that  report  the  error  status  in  BS_NURBC  reception  were  interfered  by  the  same
interference  source  identified  in  the  BS-NURBC  message,  then  the  OBS  should  update  the  database  and
reply to the SSs that have sent the error report. (See Figure 15-15.)

In any case, if the new BS cannot find the BSIS, it should start an ad-hoc method to find the neighborhood
topology. The entering BS uses the CSI to broadcast its network address to the reachable SSs in the neighbor
systems.  Once  the  SSs  received  this  signaling,  they  should  report  to  their  serving  BS  one  by  one
unsolicitedly, the information of the new BS and the interference status that they record during the reception
should be reported to the serving BS.

The serving BS should get all the information from the related SSs and should save the useful content in its
database. After that, the serving BS should contact new BSs using the network address reported by the SS
and transfer the parameter of its own database to the new one with authorization and negotiation, thereafter
the serving BS should also get the parameters and other corresponding information from the new BS.

15.3.4.3 BS Neighborhood Update Request BroadCasting (BS_NURBC)

The BS_NURBC message is a dedicated signaling sequence broadcast by the initializing BS or the operating
BS  using  either  CSI  subchannel  or  Subchannel  3  in  CXCC. This  message  is  used  for  basic  connectivity
creation (15.3.4.2) and for coordination between neighbor systems (15.3.4.4, 15.4.2.2, 15.4.3) without basic
connectivity in backhaul.

For  basic  connectivity  creation,  this  message  is  sent  from  the  BS  to  the  SS  in  the  coexistence  neighbor
systems. This message uses the PLD part of the CSI sequence (15.3.4.1.3) or Freq keying (15.3.5) to carry
the network address information of its network and the BSID from the BS to the SSs in neighbor systems.
The network and BSID information shall be reported by the SS to its serving coexistence neighbor BS using
CX-CSI-MNTR-REP  or  REP_RSP.  The  serving  coexistence  neighbor  BS  shall  communicate  to  the
requesting BS via the network, and proceed with further coexistence negotiation.

To prevent the BSID bits from being persistently masked by neighbor’s BSID bits during collision detection
(15.3.4.4),  TLV  with  bitwise-inverted  BSID  is  also  defined  for  BS_NURBC.  When  BS_NURBC  is
broadcast in OCSI, the CSI sequence formed by BS_NURBC with normal BSID and its bitwise-inverted
BSID are interleaved in the OCSI allocation.

An  RTK  shall  be  randomly  generated  in  the  BS  and  broadcast  using  BS_NURBC.  The  neighbor  BS
receiving  such  message,  which  sends  the  CXP  request  message  back  via  network  or  response  using
BS_NURBC,  needs  to  carry  the  RTK  in  the  relevant  message.  This  prevents  the  BS  from  being  easily
attacked by a station that has static contact information for the system, but does not have any WirelessMAN-
CX airlink capability. Table 11-77 lists the TLV encoding for the BS_NURBC message.

All  these  types  can  be  used  for  interference  identification  since  each  BS_NURBC  includes  BSID
information of its transmitting BS.

— Type  4:  NURBC_Air  is  used  for  interference  identification  (15.3.5.1)  and  broadcast  basic

information for further coordination.

— Types 5–6: 5) Channel Switch Request; 6) Channel Switch Response are used for coordination for

Master Frame allocation optimization (15.4.3).

— Types 9–10: 9) OCSI Backoff Request; 10) OCSI Backoff Response are used for OCSI collision

detection and resolution (15.3.4.4).

The monitoring on ICSI is for the SS to discover the initializing BS by decoding the signaling within ICSI
broadcast from the initializing neighbor BS (see 15.3.4.2). The BS shall set the monitoring mode of all SS on
each OCSI allocation, using CSI Monitoring Configure (CX-CSI-MNTR-CFG) message (see 6.3.2.3.94) to
support OCSI collision detection and resolution.

While one OCSI allocation is monitored, the monitoring has two modes based on the status of the OCSI
collision detection, collision detection mode, and collision backoff mode.

In OCSI collision detection mode, the SS monitors the interference level on symbol duration known as bit
zero in BSID field or bit-converse BSID field (see 15.3.4.1.1), which is supposed to have only noise without
other neighbor’s signal during the same interval. When the SS discovers that the interference level during at
least one monitoring zero symbols in the CSI sequence is above the interference criteria, this sequence in
such OCSI allocation is marked with collision suspicion within the SS. When two or more CSI sequences
within the recent four CSI sequences in the same OCSI allocation is marked with collision suspicion, the SS
should  report  to  its  serving  BS,  using  a  CSI  monitoring  report  (CX-CSI-MNTR-REP)  message  (see
6.3.2.3.95). So that the serving BS or the according known neighbor occupying this OCSI allocation can
enter  the  backoff  mode  and  request  the  SSs  to  proceed  with  OCSI  monitoring  to  identify  the  unknown
neighbor. The BS should broadcast the CX-CSI-MNTR-CFG to the SSs containing the BSID of the known
BS occupying this OCSI allocation, so that the SS can easily find the symbol duration that is supposed to be
zero  bit  in  the  BSID  field  or  bitwise-inverted  BSID  field  according  to  the  predefined  signaling  message
structure (see 15.3.4.1.3, 15.3.4.3).

Authorized licensed use limited to: John Greninger. Downloaded on April 01,2019 at 05:32:44 UTC from IEEE Xplore.  Restrictions apply.

2455
Copyright © 2018 IEEE. All rights reserved.

IEEE Std 802.16-2017
IEEE Standard for Air Interface for Broadband Wireless Access Systems

In OCSI collision backoff mode, the original occupying BS should broadcast the signaling message in the
backoff window only one time, because most of the time the OCSI should not be occupied by the original
occupying BS. Therefore, the SS is able to receive the signaling from its new neighbor system, and decodes
the information other than the original OCSI payload. After that, the system may negotiate with the newly
discovered and identified neighbor.

When the collision is solved or the backoff timer expired, the BS should reconfigure the CSI monitoring
mode using CX-CSI-MNTR-CFG message (see 6.3.2.3.94). The OCSI backoff resolution shall be based on
a truncated binary exponential backoff, with the initial backoff window and the maximum backoff window
selected by the BS. While in backoff mode, the BS shall count down the backoff window and request the SS
to switch monitoring mode accordingly. If the BS occupying the OCSI allocation is a known neighbor BS,
the serving BS shall contact that neighbor BS using the network or BS_NURBC to request that it enter into
a backoff mode before transmitting, and the requested neighbor BS shall response according to its action.

The backoff window was initialized as a selected power-of-two value (see 10.5.2) representing the number
of signaling message broadcast durations (256  CSI_cycle CX-Frames). The BS shall randomly choose one
CSI  sequence  allocation  out  of  all  the  allocations  in  the  backoff  window  to  broadcast  the  message,  and
remain  silent  for  the  other  OCSI  allocations  within  the  backoff  window. Therefore,  most  of  the  time  the
signaling message from the serving BS in the backoff window will not collide with the signaling message
from a neighbor BS that had the same initial OCSI allocation.

The reason the BS is not silent during the entire backoff window is to avoid a deadlock scenario in which
two  neighboring  systems  detect  a  collision  at  the  same  time,  and  both  become  silent  during  the  entire
broadcast  window.  In  this  case,  the  backoff  window  should  increase  until  it  reaches  its  maximum  upper
limit.

15.3.5 Interferer identification

The interferer may be identified using CXCC procedures or using Interference Evaluation Burst procedures
or through a reciprocal interference estimation.

15.3.5.1 Interferer identification using CXCC

The interfering base station may be identified from the BSID information, which is included in any of the
following:

— BSD transmitted during the CXCC subchannel 2
— BS_NURBC messages transmitted during CXCC subchannel 3
— CSI subchannel

The interfering SS may be identified from the SSID information, which is included in SSURF message and
transmitted during CXCC subchannel 2.

15.3.5.2 Scheduled interference evaluation

This  mechanism  uses  the  Interference  Evaluation  Burst  for  the  evaluation  of  the  interference  created  by
transmitters belonging to other systems, during the Master subframe of the system requesting the evaluation.

The  Interference  Evaluation  Burst  shall  consist  of  a  short  regular  data  transmission.  The  Interference
Evaluation Burst is scheduled using the over-the-air (15.5) or over-the-backbone (15.6) CXP for intersystem
communication and the CX-DL-MAP and CX-UL-MAP messages. The relevant CXP messages are either
CX-FWD-REQ (Action Code: Evaluate Interference Request) or the primitive C-CX-REQ (Action_Type =
Evaluate  Interference),  which  use  assigned  Interference  Evaluation  Burst  (IEB)  identifiers  to  each  IEB
transmission slot.

Authorized licensed use limited to: John Greninger. Downloaded on April 01,2019 at 05:32:44 UTC from IEEE Xplore.  Restrictions apply.

2456
Copyright © 2018 IEEE. All rights reserved.

IEEE Std 802.16-2017
IEEE Standard for Air Interface for Broadband Wireless Access Systems

Every transmitter should send its Interference Evaluation Burst during an interference-free slot. The time
position of this slot is associated with an Interference Evaluation Burst identifier.

The scheduling of the Interference Evaluation Burst transmission shall not use the CSI allocation.

A  receiver  shall  listen  to  the  media  during  the  Interference  Evaluation  Burst  slots.  An  interference
measurement of the signal received during those slots will give an estimate of the interference level created
by  the  scheduled  IEB  transmitters.  This  interference  estimate  may  be  used  by  the  Master  BSs  for
determining the requested power reduction to be used in the relevant CXP messages in 15.5 and 15.6. The
IEB identifiers associated with transmissions creating the strongest interference levels can be further used in
procedures for mitigating the interference (see 15.4.4). During the allocated Interference Evaluation Burst
transmit opportunity no other radio transmitters should operate. The silent transmitters shall schedule a GAP
DIUC or UIUC IE.

An SS will report the measurement results using the REP REQ/RESP messages.

The  base  station  database  should  keep  the  following  information  regarding  the  usage  of  the  Master
subframes belonging to other systems:

— BS power, relative to the Interference Evaluation Burst power, when using each of the subframes

(Master, Slave, Common)

— List  of  SSs  and  their  power,  relative  to  the  Interference  Evaluation  Burst  power,  when  using

different subframes

The received power from a certain radio transmitter is known, based on the Interference Evaluation Burst
approach,  only  during  the  Master  subframe.  The  received  power  from  the  same  transmitter,  during  other
subframes, can be obtained by using the Interference Evaluation Burst measurement in the Master subframe
and  by  performing  suitable  calculations,  according  to  the  database  information  on  used  powers  in  other
subframes. The calculation should consider that the path-loss remains the same during the Master, Slave,
and Shared subframes.

15.3.5.2.1 Interference Evaluation Burst scheduling

During  some  of  the  Master  subframes,  the  base  station  shall  create  a  slot,  possibly  not  overlapping  with
another slot of a coexistence neighbor base station, during which every transmitter (BS or associated SS)
shall send the Interference Evaluation Burst that shall be used to measure the interference created by that
transmitter.

— The  “Interference  Evaluation  Burst  slot”  for  a  base  station  shall  be  created  during  its  DL  Master

subframe and the following rules apply within the Coexistence Community:
— Only one base station in a CX Community can have a scheduled Interference Evaluation Burst

transmission.

— No other BS shall transmit during this time interval, including other base stations which use

the subframe as Master.

— The “Interference Evaluation Burst slot” for a SS shall be created during the UL Master subframe

and the following rules apply:
— Only  one  SS  in  a  CX  Community  can  have  a  scheduled  Interference  Evaluation  Burst

transmission.

— No other SS shall transmit during this time interval, including other SSs that use the subframe

as Master.

— The MAC messages for scheduling both the Interference Evaluation Bursts and the silence intervals
during the transmission of the Interference Evaluation Bursts are CX-UL-MAP and CX-DL-MAP,
using suitable UIUC/DIUC.

15.3.5.3 Reciprocal interference estimation

15.3.5.3.1 Reciprocal uplink interference estimation

After detecting a neighbor BS creating interference, a SS shall report the interference power of this neighbor
BS to its serving BS. The serving BS can estimate the uplink interference power caused by the SS to its
neighbor BS (ISS_NBS) based the interference detection report from this SS, using Equation (15-1).

15.4 Interference prevention

This subclause describes the methods of preventing the interference between IEEE 802.16 systems operating
in license-exempt bands, based on the interference information that the system had identified (see 15.3) and
a Coexistence Frame structure described in this clause.

A set of rules are defined in 15.4.1 that ensure efficient interference prevention. A CX-CBP is defined for
sharing the wireless medium in combined scheduled and contention-based mode.

The time-frequency spectrum allocations to every system can be optimized using the procedures in 15.4.2
and  15.4.3. These  procedures allow  an  optimized  channel and subframe  distribution, having as  scope  the
interference reduction during operation and increased spectral efficiency of the shared spectrum.

The spectral efficiency may be further improved by using the Slave subframes, as described in 15.4.4.

The  spectrum  resource  in  time  domain  may  be  allocated  dynamically  between  the  systems  by  using  the
Credit Token Protocol in 15.4.5.

15.4.1 Coexistence frame

15.4.1.1 Overview

Multiple  systems  coexisting  within  one  channel  shall  share  the  radio  resource  of  the  channel  in  the  time
domain,  preventing  intersystem  interference.  The  systems  may  cooperate  by  exchanging  relevant
information and negotiating fairly.

The sharing mechanism is facilitated by scheduling in a fair fashion, and reallocating the resource within the
channel in the time domain to obtain better overall network capacity.

The system shall classify all the systems in the community as interfering/not interfering units and all the SSs
as interfered/not interfered for various purposes.

For  all  the  neighbor  systems  (which  can  be  either  an  interference  victim  or  a  source  in  any  one  of  the
candidate  channels),  the  initializing  BS  shall  group  them  all  as  potentially  interfering  systems  before
choosing the operational channel. When the initializing BS has selected the operational channel, only the
neighbor  systems  that  are  interfering  in  the  current  channel  should  be  grouped  as  interfering  neighbor
systems. The other neighbor systems should be maintained in the database, for the case of such as channel
reallocation coordination.

As for all the SSs associated with the serving systems, the BS should group them into interfering or non-
interfering ones, according to their operational parameters (transmission power, subchannels, modulation,
and  coding  state  etc.),  so  that  the  BS  can  schedule  their  data  traffic  into  different  subframes  to  prevent
interference.  The  SS  that  operates  such  that  it  does  not  interfere  with  other  systems  can  use  one  of  the
optional Common subframe, Shared subframe, or the Master subframe for their data traffic, while the data
traffic of SSs operating with interfering conditions should be scheduled within the Master subframe.

15.4.1.2 Scheduling of interference free intervals in the context of IEEE 802.16 MAC

A CX-Frame is created by a sequence of four IEEE 802.16 MAC frames and it is subdivided into specific
subframes (see Figure 15-20).

The CX-Frame is composed of Master, Slave, and Shared subframes, which can be used for DL or for UL
(see Figure 15-19) and the optional Common subframe, which may be used in DL only (see Figure 15-20).

During the Common and the Shared subframes, the communication not affected by interference should be
scheduled.

Figure 15-21 indicates the recommended CX-Frame if a frequency channel accommodates only two Master
frames.  Each  Master  frame  is  followed  by  a  Shared  frame.  It  is  recommended  that  an  operator  will  use
systematically the same Master frame. The uplink scheduling can be done using the CX-UL-MAP message
or the regular UL-MAP message with shorter relevance.

15.4.1.3 General rules

This standard gives support for multiple Master/Slave/Shared configurations inside the CX-Frame. The BS
can  establish  the  Master/Slave/Shared  subframes  for  DL  and  UL  in  a  flexible  mode,  by  using  the  TLVs
named “CX Frame usage” within DCD (11.4.1) and UCD (11.3.1) messages, respectively.

The rules for occupying the Master subframes are as follows:

— Only systems synchronized with the GPS or equivalent time source shall act as Masters.
— Systems that do not qualify for using Master subframes in a specific channel shall either not operate

in that channel or shall limit their transmission to Shared subframes.

— The first WirelessMAN-CX system in an area should use the first Master subframe defined in the
CX-Frame, while the second WirelessMAN-CX system should use the second Master subframe.
— The Master systems shall claim a Master subframe by either inserting their Interference Evaluation
Burst in subchannel 4, the coexistence messages in subchannel 2, or the coexistence signaling in the
CSI subchannel of the CXCC. No system is allowed to claim more than one Master subframe.
— If  interference  is  detected,  having  as  source  non-SSUs,  the  CX  frame  structure  shall  be  changed
according  to  15.4.1.4.1.  If  no  non-SSU  systems  are  detected,  the  CX-Frame  should  have  the
structure in 15.4.1.2.

The rule for operation during subframes, which are not yet occupied is as follows:

— The subframes not yet occupied shall be considered as Shared subframes.

The following rules apply to Slave systems, using WirelessMAN-CX technologies:

— The  Slave systems to WirelessMAN-CX Masters  may transmit only  if they comply to one of  the

following conditions:
— Are  provisioned  by  operators  for  usage  of  the  Slave  subframes;  in  this  case  the  operators

assume the responsibility of not interfering with the Master subframes.

Authorized licensed use limited to: John Greninger. Downloaded on April 01,2019 at 05:32:44 UTC from IEEE Xplore.  Restrictions apply.

2463
