IEEE Std 802.16-2017
IEEE Standard for Air Interface for Broadband Wireless Access Systems

— Implement  CXP  messages  for  intersystem  communication  including  the  CXP  messages  that

reduce their operating powers, including the request to stop the operation.

The operational rules related to the power control are as follows:

— The  transmission  power  during  the  Shared  subframe  should  be  6 dB  less  than  the  power  in  the
Master subframe. The power rule may be broadcast using the UCD and DCD messages. The TLVs
named Power attenuation in CX-Frame, defined within DCD (11.4.1) and UCD (11.3.1) messages,
allow more flexibility regarding the transmitted powers within the CX-Frame. The BS may, based
on the interference evaluation, set different power rules within the different subframes. For example,
two systems may alternatively use higher powers during the Shared frame. Let’s address the case
with two Masters in Figure 15-21. During the Shared frame 4N + 1, the System 1 power attenuation
may be 3 dB, while the System 2 power attenuation may be 6 dB. During the Shared frame 4N + 3,
the System 1 power attenuation may be 6 dB, while the System 2 power attenuation may be 3 dB.

The  detection  of  non-SSU  systems  should  be  based  on  interference  measurement  during  CXCC.  Three
thresholds are defined within DCD TLVs (11.4.1) and UCD TLVs (11.3.1): the SSU detection threshold (one
for  significantly  higher  power  SSU  and  one  for  similar  or  lower  power  SSU)  and  a  non-SSU  detection
threshold. The relevant TLVs are as follows:

— SSU-H threshold
— SSU-L threshold
— Non-SSU threshold

In order to enable service to regions in which two Slave systems overlap, a hierarchy structure should be
applied among the Slaves, as follows:

Let S1 denote the Master system of the first frame (MAC_Frame = 4N), S2 the Master system of the second
frame (MAC Frame 4N + 1), and S3 the Master system of the third frame (MAC Frame 4N + 2). In one CX
Frame the system’s priority shall be demoted from frame to frame as follows:

— In MAC frame number 4N, S3 shall be the secondary Master in the frame
— In MAC Frame 4N + 1, S1 shall be the secondary Master
— In MAC Frame 4N + 2, S2 shall be the secondary Master

In the following CX-Frame, the system’s priority shall be promoted from frame to frame as follows:

— In MAC Frame 4(N + 1), S2 shall be the secondary Master
— In MAC Frame 4(N + 1) + 1, S3 shall be the secondary Master
— In MAC Frame 4(N + 1) + 2, S1 shall be the secondary Master

When system Si has priority over system Sj, it means that system Sj shall not transmit a signal that would
interfere with any SS of system Si.

Figure 15-24 shows the priority order for three systems in different subframe structures. The common parts
and TX/RX boundaries are omitted. The arrows show the priority demotion and promotion for system S1.

If two systems create interference one to each other during their Slave subframes, the system having lower
“rank” may be requested to reduce its operating power by the system having a higher rank.

15.4.1.4 Coordinated Contention-Based Protocol

This subclause only applies to license-exempt frequency bands allocated by national/regional/international
regulations for primary services using bursty systems.

15.4.1.4.1 Frame structure for CX-CBP

The approach for interference avoidance between WirelessMAN-CX systems is based on the CX-Frame in
Figure 15-25, where no more than two WirelessMAN-CX systems can share a frequency channel if a bursty
system  is  detected.  The  CX-Frame  leaves  transmission  opportunity  to  bursty  systems,  such  that  the
probability  of  good  performance  of  IEEE  802.16  systems  in  license-exempt  bands  is  increased.  The
WirelessMAN-CX  system  should  detect  the  existence  of  non-SSU  systems  in  the  band  based  on
measurements during the dedicated CXCC slots.

The following occupancy rules for the Master and Shared subframes are defined:

— MAC  Frames  4N  and  4N + 1  are  reserved  for  scheduled  operation;  the  time  interval  is  named

CXSBI (Coordinated Coexistence Schedule-Based Interval)

— MAC  Frames  4N + 2  and  4N + 3  are  reserved  for  bursty  operation;  the  time  interval  is  named
Coordinated  Coexistence  Contention-Based  Interval  (CXCBI).  During  CXCBI,  there  are  no
common subframes;

— The scheduled systems using the channel may use the MAC Frames reserved for bursty operation in

a Coordinated Coexistence Contention-Based Protocol (CX-CBP) mode, as defined below.

The CX-Frame structure when there are three systems on a channel is in Figure 15-25.

In case of only two systems on a channel, from which one system is bursty, the IEEE 802.16 system can use
the CXSBI as Master.

a)

Rules for operation during CXSBI
The operational rules related to adaptive modulation/coding and power control are as follows:
— The modulation used during the Master/Slave subframes should be chosen such that the full
subframe duration is used for data transmission; this will better protect the WirelessMAN-CX
Master  subframes  from  the  interference  created  by  bursty  systems,  which  can  detect  short
silence intervals, start their transmissions, and overlap with the next Master subframe.
— The  power  of  the  transmitters  shall  be  minimized  to  the  level  required  for  stable  data

communication.

b)

Rules for operation during the CXCBI time interval
During CXCBI a special form of the Contention-Based Protocol, named “Coordinated Coexistence
Contention-Based Protocol” or CX-CBP shall be used.

15.4.1.4.2 CX-CBP description

The Coordinated Coexistence Contention-Based Protocol (CX-CBP) has the following basic elements:

— Frame structure derived from the CX-Frame
— Detection of bursty systems
— Scheduled listen-before-talk (SLBT)
— Coexistence contention window (CXCW) and quiet periods (QP)

Authorized licensed use limited to: John Greninger. Downloaded on April 01,2019 at 05:32:44 UTC from IEEE Xplore.  Restrictions apply.

— Logarithmic back-off
— Determination and scheduling of the transmit opportunities
— Longer slots as compared with those used by bursty systems

a) CX-CBP: Operation at CXCBI start

During a specified time named CXLBTStart, no IEEE 802.16 activity may take place. This allows
the detection with high probability of the bursty systems deployed in the area by either BS or SS.
The energy for detection of bursty systems is identical to the energy for detection in SLBT mode.
The REP-RSP (6.3.2.3.33) MAC message conveys the information related to the existence of the
bursty system from SS to the BS. If no bursty system activity is detected for T_Bursty_Detect by a
system, that system may switch to the CX-Frame structure described in 15.4.1.2.
The duration of the CXLBTStart shall be higher than the CX_LBT_Start_Min, defined in 10.5.3.
CXLBTStart includes the RTG interval before a downlink transmission.
The CXSlotTime is equivalent to one OFDM symbol time or the duration of the DLSlot (8.4.3.1) for
the OFDMA PHY. This time includes medium sensing, Tx/Rx turn-around time, propagation delay,
and processing delay.

b) CX-CBP: Scheduled listen-before-talk (SLBT)

Before any transmission during CXCBI, an IEEE 802.16 BS shall check if the medium is free.
The following rules shall apply:
— If the medium is free for at least CX_LBT_Time, before the scheduled transmission time of an
IEEE 802.16 device, the IEEE 802.16-based system shall start its transmission at the scheduled
time.

— If the medium is busy, the transmission shall be deferred until the next scheduled transmission

opportunity.

— The  SLBT  threshold  is  –85  dBm  for  every  MHz  of  channel  width,  for  example  the  SLBT

threshold for 10 MHz channel is –75 dBm.

c) CX-CBP: Transmission scheduling

— The duration of the allocated interval for transmission, using either the DL MAP or UL MAP
allocations  shall  be  suitable  to  DL/UL  subframe  synchronization.  This  condition  ensures
compatibility  with  IEEE  802.16  MAC  and  better  coexistence  between  WirelessMAN-CX
systems in case of adjacent areas using CX-Frames according to Figure 15-19 or according to
Figure 15-25.

— The  CX-DL-MAP  and  CX-UL-MAP  messages  should  be  used  for  scheduling  the  traffic  in
MAC frames either for extended relevance or for scheduling conditional transmissions. These
messages have an enlarged scope and allow the support of MAC frames using SLBT.

— All the BS transmissions during CXCBI shall use SLBT. The first DL data burst transmitted in
a  frame  should  start  with  a  preamble  transmission,  pre-scheduled  in  the  CX-DL-MAP
message. MAPs may be transmitted, if they are pre-scheduled within CX-DL-MAP message.

— SS should also implement SLBT.
An  example  of  scheduling  DL  listen-before-talk  opportunities  inside  the  CXCW  is  given  in
Figure 15-26,  which  shows  the  extended  MAP  relevance  for  covering  the  whole  duration  of  the
contention window.
Figure 15-27 shows an example of scheduling for UL SLBT opportunities inside the CXCW. It was
preferred to reduce the relevance of the MAP such to better adapt the transmission opportunities to
the actual UL traffic.

d) CX-CBP: Contention window

The contention window mechanism enables multiple devices to access the medium, while reducing
the collisions.
The  random  number  of  slots  before  a  scheduled  transmission  is  shown  as  slanted  lines  in
Figure 15-26 and Figure 15-27.
The contention windows shall start after the expiration of the CXLBT Start interval. The duration of
the contention window for a particular IEEE 802.16 transmitter is as follows:
— CXCWmin = 7  CXSlotTime
— CXCWmin < CXCW < CXCWmax
CXCWmax is a system parameter having the CXSlotTime as unit and that is calculated separately
for DL and for UL. CXCWmax cannot cover more than 2 CXCBI concatenated intervals.
The conditional transmission opportunity is scheduled during a random slot chosen within the CW.
The transmitter shall assess before the scheduled transmission time if the medium is free, based on
SLBT procedures.
Figure 15-26 shows the DL scheduling of conditional transmission opportunities inside the CXCW.
The  IE  that  actually  schedules  conditional  transmission  opportunities  during  the  CXCBI  shall  be
inserted  in  DL  or  UL  CX-MAPs  transmitted  during  any  of  the  Common,  Master,  or  Slave
subframes.

e) CX-CBP: Back-off mechanisms

f)

In case of unsuccessful reception, the following back-off mechanisms are defined:
— Logarithmic back-off mechanism based on the exponential increase of the CXCW size
— Additional back-off mechanism inserting quiet periods
CX-CBP: Exponential CXCW and quiet periods
In the case of failed receptions, the base station shall increase the CW for DL or UL traffic according
to the rule:
— CXCW_New = 2  CXCW_Old + 1
where CXCW_New is the number of slots in the CW after back-off and CXCW_Old is the number
of slots in the CW before back-off.
— CXCWNew < CXCWmax
The conditional transmission opportunities that do not fall in intervals suitable for DL transmission
from BS and UL transmission from the SS shall not be used.
In case of a successful reception, the CXCW to be used in the next scheduling of the transmissions
shall be CXCWmin.
If  more  than  one  LBT-TXOP  is  scheduled  during  a  DL  or  UL  subframe,  the  two  zones  shall  be
separated by a CXCW.
If the CW has reached its maximum value and the last transmission was not successfully received,
those conditioned transmission opportunities scheduled within first CXCBI shall be skipped and a
quiet period shall be inserted during this interval.
If the next transmission is also unsuccessful, the next two CXCBI intervals shall be considered as
quiet periods and the next transmission shall be scheduled using the maximum contention window
only.
Table 15-4  and  Table 15-5  illustrate  the  DL  process  of  CXCW  logarithmic  back-off,  for  a  5 ms
OFDMA Frame with 47 symbols, 60% DL, 40% UL including 28 symbols in DL and 19 symbols in
UL.
For simplicity, let’s suppose that the conditional transmission interval is scheduled as LBT-TXOP,
with  a  minimum  duration  of  10  symbols.  It is  assumed  that  it  is  used  with  DL  FUSC,  using  1
symbol/slot.

g) Determination and scheduling of the conditional transmission opportunities

The scheduling of a LBT-TXOP during CXCBI shall comply with the following rules:
— M (default = 2) next CXCBI intervals are concatenated.
— Concatenation shall take into consideration the DL and UL intervals synchronization; only the

transmission opportunities for BS or SS consistent with DL or UL shall be used.
— The symbols intended for CXLBTStart at the beginning of each CXCBI are skipped.
— The  OFDM/OFDMA  symbols  in  the  concatenated  CXCBI  intervals  shall  be  numbered,
according to the rules used in IEEE Std 802.16 (excluding the TTG and RTG intervals).

15.4.1.5 CX-Frame Legacy SS support

Possible methods to support legacy SSs are described in the following subclauses.

15.4.1.5.1 Method A

For SSs that do not support CX-Frame usage, the resource allocation should be scheduled within each CX-
frame in WirelessMAN-CX systems. The Preambles and MAPs should only be transmitted in the DL Master
subframes. The MAPs in Master subframes should be used to indicate the resource allocation of this system
in a CX-Frame, possibly including the resource schedule in the Master subframe, Shared subframe, Slave
subframe, CX-CBP subframe (see 15.4.1.4.2), and optional common subframe.

15.4.2 Working channel allocation optimization

This subclause describes the method of Adaptive Channel Selection (ACS) to prevent interference. The first
step  is  to  attempt  to  identify  a  vacant  channel  using  the  gathered  information  from  the  system  and  the
neighbor systems (see Annex Q). If a vacant channel is not found, the BS then tries to obtain an exclusive
channel by optimization of channel distribution (see 15.4.2.1and 15.4.2.2).

The  success  of  either  step  will  enable  the  BS  to  start  working  with  an  exclusive  working  channel.  If  no
vacant channel can be found, then the BS should attempt the channel sharing coordination procedure.

15.4.2.1 How to select a free channel (for ACS and DFS)

After scanning and before interference identification, the IBS should try to figure out whether it interferes
with other systems in each of these candidate channels. In the initialization phase of an IBS, its neighbors
should  send  their  current  working  channel  allocation,  neighbors’  working  channel  allocations,  OCSI
allocation, and subframe allocation using CXP messages, as well as a flag having alternative channels. By
the feedback messages received after the signaling broadcasting, the IBS should collect the information of
its interference victims on each channel.

If  there  is  neither  interference  detected  nor  interference  victims  found  using  interference  assessment  by
active scanning (15.3.2) in some channel by the IBS, the channel is marked as a “free” channel of the IBS.
When the IBS can find non-interfering channels at the initialization phase, it shall select its working channel
as follows:

— If the IBS can find non-interfering channels that are also its 2-hop neighbors’ working channels, it

randomly selects one from those non-interfering channels as its working channel.

— Otherwise the IBS randomly selects one from all available non-interfering channels as its working

channel.

When the IBS cannot find any non-interfering channel, the IBS should figure out whether a “free” channel
can be vacated by optimized channel distribution, as described in 15.4.2.2.

The process of ACS is shown in Figure 15-30. The ACS process concludes with either one of two possible
results: 1) a “free” channel is validated with or without channel distribution optimization, or 2) no “free”
channel.

15.4.2.2 Optimization of channel distribution

In the initialization phase of an IBS, its neighbors shall send their current working channel allocation, OCSI
allocation and subframe allocation using CXP messages or signaling (BS_NURBC), as well as indications
of alternative channels flag and alternative subframe flag. The IBS maintains the channel information of all
1-hop and 2-hop neighbors in the BS information table.

When the IBS cannot find any free channel at the initialization phase, it should try to change the channel
distribution and to vacate a free channel by switching some of its neighbors’ working channels to others.

First, the IBS examines all the channels and identifies which neighbors operating on them have alternative
channels for the system, and sorts them according to the number of neighbor systems working on each.

Second, the IBS selects one of the channels used by the fewest BS, and considers this channel as its potential
working channel. The IBS should now negotiate with all the neighbors working on the selected channel.

Third, to negotiate with every neighbor BS working on this channel, the IBS should send a channel switch
request (see 15.5.3.24, 15.3.4.3 type 5) message to each. A neighbor OBS, which has received this message
should  select  one  of  its  alternative  channels  as  its  target  working  channel,  and  try  to  move  its  working
channel  to  that  channel  as  long  as  the  request  is  valid. After  the  working  channel  was  switched  to  its
alternative, the neighbor OBS should acknowledge the switch to the IBS by sending back a channel switch
response (see 15.5.3.25, 15.3.4.3 type 6) message with success indication, otherwise it should send back a
fail indication. If the IBS received any rejection from the neighbors, to which the IBS had sent the request,
the  IBS  should  cancel  the  request  by  sending  another  message  with  the  rolling  back  indication  for  the
neighbors to switch back to the channel they used before the IBS’s channel switching request.

Finally, when the IBS receives positive acknowledge messages from all of its neighbor OBSs, it means the
channel redistribution optimization procedure has succeeded to vacate a channel for the IBS, and the IBS
should use it as a working channel afterwards. Otherwise, the IBS should try to vacate the next potential
channel.

If the channel redistribution procedure fails and all the potential channels cannot be vacated to become the
IBS’s working channel, the IBS shall try to share one channel with some of its neighbors.

If  the  channel  redistribution  procedure  succeeds,  a  list  of  alternative  channels  of  related  BSs  should  be
updated  if  their  neighbors  have  changed  their  working  channels.  The  IBS  should  broadcast  to  all  its
neighbors  that  it  will  be  working  on  the  selected  channel. All  its  neighbors  should  add  it  as  their  new
neighbor  in  the  BS  information  table  and  exclude  its  target  working  channel  from  the  list  of  potential
alternative channels. The neighbor OBSs that moved away from this channel should also notify the change
to all of their neighbors, so their neighbors can update the distributed database according to the change.

The above process of channel selection optimization is shown in Figure 15-31.

15.4.3 Master Frame allocation optimization

When WirelessMAN-CX system has to share a channel with its neighbor system, it shall select a subframe
acting  as  its  Master  subframe.  By  checking  the  information  table  (see  Annex Q),  if  it  can  find  some
subframes  free  in  any  channel  it  can  use  in  its  neighborhood,  it  can  randomly  choose  one  of  them  as  its
Master subframe and start operation.

When not able to find a free subframe currently, the system shall check in any of its available channels to see
if  there  is  some  subframe  on  which  all  the  neighbor  systems  using  it  as  the  Master  subframe  have  an
alternative subframe (ALTSF). The system can negotiate with the systems occupying one of these subframes
to  move  to  their ALTSF  and  vacate  a  subframe  for  itself  without  changing  the  current  structure  of  the
WirelessMAN-CX-Frame.

The system shall check the candidate subframe one by one and negotiate with its neighbors to move their
Master subframes to their ALTSFs. If the system succeeds in finding a free subframe, it can take it as its
Master subframe; otherwise, it should try to search for another channel, or consider operating as a Slave.
A flow  chart  describing  the  procedure  to  find  a  vacant  subframe  to  operate  as  a  Master  is  shown  in
Figure 15-32. See Figure 15-33 for the process of optimizing subframe distribution.

Every BS maintains the status of its ALTSFs by itself. It counts up all the vacant subframes within the CX-
Frame (see Figure 15-20) as ALTSFs, which can be used as Master subframes. The BSs should count up the
number of its ALTSFs by scanning and contacting all coexistence neighbors. Resource IDs for every ALTSF
are  also  stored  in  the  distributed  database. All  the  channels  that  are  not  usable  shall  be  ignored.  This
information shall be maintained in the information table in the distributed database.

Using  CXP  messages  or  signaling  (BS_NURBC)  in  communicating  with  the  systems  inside  the
neighborhood,  the  BS  can  learn  whether  its  neighbor  has  ALTSF  and  set  an  indication  flag  for  each
neighbor. This information will help the BS to find a neighbor system with which it can negotiate.

After  finding  all  the  subframes  for  which  there  is  an  ALTSF  to  all  the  systems  using  them  as  Master
subframes, the system can sort the subframes by the number of neighbors working on each and add them to
a  potential  subframe  list.  Every  time  the  system  should  choose  a  subframe  with  the  smallest  number  of
neighbors using it as Master subframe and negotiate with these neighbors, using Master subframe Switch
Request  message  (see  15.5.3.26,  15.3.4.3  type  7)  to  request  the  neighbor  systems  currently  using  this
subframe as its Master subframe to switch to one of its ALTSF. If all the requests succeed by getting Master
subframe Switch Response message (see 15.5.3.27, 15.3.4.3 type 8), the system can switch to this channel

and start to use this subframe as its Master subframe; otherwise, the system needs to ask all the neighbors to
keep using their original subframe by using another Master subframe Switch Request message with rolling
back indication. It shall delete the subframe from the potential subframe list and continue to negotiate on
another potential subframe. If all the potential subframes in the list have been checked and no one can be
vacated as Master subframe of the system, the process has failed. Even though the process has failed, it may
be possible for the network of WirelessMAN-CX neighborhoods to be configured with a new set of Master
subframe allocations that create a vacant subframe for the requesting WirelessMAN-CX system. In such a
case, the WirelessMAN-CX system can use this vacant subframe as a Master subframe, and the process will
succeed.  This  possibility  can  be  achieved  through  a  multiple  hop  procedure.  For  example,  in  a  two-hop
procedure, the WirelessMAN-CX system can learn the ALTSFs of the neighbors for each of its neighbors.
By requesting some of the neighbors of each neighbor to move to their ALTSFs, the immediate neighbors of
the WirelessMAN-CX system may then move to an ALTSF that was otherwise blocked. This process can be
repeated out to as many hops from the WirelessMAN-CX system as may be required to create an available
Master subframe.

15.4.4 Interference control in subframes

The interference control may operate during Slave or Shared subframes. The interference control procedures
should use interferer identification as described in 15.3.5.

A  BS  has  the  right  to  request  any  interferer  to  reduce  its  power  by  P  dB,  for  transmissions  during  the
subframes in which this base station is the Master. If the requested transmitter cannot execute the request, it
shall cease its operation during the Master subframe of the requesting base station. The system that uses the
subframe  as  a  Master  may  use  the  maximum  capable  and  allowed  operating  EIRP  with  no  limitation.  If
allowed by the operating Master system, a newly entering system may use this subframe at its maximum
capable  and  allowed  operating  EIRP;  otherwise,  it  shall  reduce  its  power  to  a  level  acceptable  by  the
operating Master system using the subframe as Master. The operating Master system can deny the operation
of any other system in parallel, if this causes harmful interference to it.

Control primitives or inter-BS messages having as Action Type “Reduce Power or Quit Subframe” or “Work
as Slave” should be used for controlling the interference levels.

An acceptable interference level during a Master subframe should be lower than 3 dB above the noise or
12 dB below the signal.

The procedures for controlling the interference to BS are as follows:

— Identification of the source of interference, using the procedures defined in 15.3.5.
— Request for transmit power reduction using CXP messages in 15.6. If the sources of the interference
are identified, the BS should send a message to the BSs of the interfering systems, asking them to
drop the power of the specified transmitter inside the neighbor systems by P dB.

— Request for stopping the operation. Alternatively, the BS could send a message to the BSs of the
interference source systems, asking the interference source system to stop operating during this BS’s
Master slot.

The procedures for controlling the interference to SS are as follows:

— Request SS Reports in the available Frames

— CINR Report, by using the Frame Specific SINR Report in 11.11.

— Reschedule the SS operation such to avoid the interference.

The interference status information of this BS in the system and the interference status information in the
coexistence message from its neighbor systems should be stored and updated regularly into the distributed
database of this system.

15.4.5 Credit Token-Based Coexistence Protocol (CT-CXP)

In some traffic circumstances, some Master subframes are temporarily under-used by some BS (offering BS,
namely offerer) due to some low traffic activity while some of its neighboring BSs (requesting BS, namely
requester) require temporarily some additional Master subframe capacity to face some traffic increase. With
respect  to  this,  Master  subframe  sharing  between  neighboring  systems  contributes  for  better  spectrum
efficiency. The typical operation of sharing is illustrated in Figure 15-34 and Figure 15-35 where system S1
proposes to rent out its assigned last OFDM symbols (for a time duration T_renting_subframe per Master
subframe over several consecutive CX-Frames of total time duration T_renting_epoch) to system S2 and S3.
This Master subframe sharing is supported by the credit token based coexistence protocol (CT-CXP). CT-
CXP provides the means for an offerer to rent out temporarily some of its Master subframe capacity to some
competing  requester(s)  willing  to  rent  in  simultaneously  this  proposed  additional  resource.  CT-CXP
guarantees  exclusive  access  of  the  offerer’s  unused  Master  subframe  resource  to  the  requester(s)  for  an
agreed time period between the offerer and the requester. During this agreed period, the requester is granted
with the resource during which the offerer should not use the resource. Also, CT-CXP ensures over time a
fair access of the offerer’s Master subframe available resource between competing requesters.

15.4.5.1 CT-CXP procedures

15.4.5.1.1 Whole CT-CXP procedure

CT-CXP can be instantiated either in a non-negotiated mode or in a negotiated mode. This allows CT-CXP
to  be  flexibly  executed  as  a  function  of  the  context  (e.g.,  time  constraints  for  negotiation,  regulatory
spectrum sharing policies, and so forth). The followed approach is flexible in that it is scalable and it allows
a vendor differentiated implementation of non-negotiated or negotiated (of any types) based CT-CXP.

The non-negotiated mode requires the minimum messages exchange to support CT-CXP between the offerer
and  requester(s).  This  mode  requires  no  negotiation  iteration  between  the  offerer  and  requester,  and

Authorized licensed use limited to: John Greninger. Downloaded on April 01,2019 at 05:32:44 UTC from IEEE Xplore.  Restrictions apply.

2479
Copyright © 2018 IEEE. All rights reserved.

IEEE Std 802.16-2017
IEEE Standard for Air Interface for Broadband Wireless Access Systems

therefore can be applied when time availability is very limited and/or when the CT-CXP is executed through
over-the-air inter-BSs communications.

The  negotiated  mode  is  used  when  time  availability  is  enough  to  handle  several  iterations  for  the
negotiation. This mode is operated through network-based inter-BSs communications.

CT-CXP is composed of several consecutive procedures (offering advertisement, renting request, iterative
negotiation,  and  CT-CXP  resource  allocation)  as  shown  in  Figure 15-36.  For  the  sake  of  simplicity,  this
figure is only depicted for one (among multiple) requesters. Over-the-air based instantiation of CT-CXP for
the  non  negotiated  mode  is  depicted  on  the  left-hand  side  of  Figure 15-36.  The  over  network-based
instantiation of CT-CXP for the negotiation or non-negotiated mode is depicted on the right-hand side of
Figure 15-36.  Intersystem  over-the-air  messages  are  encapsulated  within  CX-FWD-REQ  and  CX-FWD-
RSP  messages  (6.3.2.3).  Intersystem  over-the-air  communications  mechanisms  are  described  in  15.5.
Primitives  related  to  network-based  instantiation  are  specified  in  15.6.  The  primitive  C-CX-REQ
(Action_Type  =  Token  Advertisement)  specifies  which  negotiation  mode  is  used  by  the  CT-CXP.  The
iterative negotiation procedure is executed only with the negotiated mode and not with the non-negotiated
mode.

Within  CT-CXP,  a  renting  resource  unit  (RRU)  is  defined  as  the  minimum  time  x  frequency  unit  (e.g.,
OFDM symbol, or a minimum number of symbols and subcarriers in  OFDMA) that can be rented in/out
between  the  offerer  and  a  requester.  RRU  time  duration  is  denoted  RRU_duration. A  Master  subframe  is
composed of a fixed amount of RRUs. The part of the offerer’s available Master subframe to be rented out is
named  rented  resource.  Consequently,  an  offerer’s  rented  resource  is  defined  as  an  amount  of  RRUs. A
credit token (CT) is the pseudo monetary unit used by CT-CXP allowing the requester to rent in a RRU to
the offerer. A RRU is charged as a number of CTs. Each BS is initially assigned with a CT budget, i.e., a
maximum  number  of  CTs.  This  maximum  number  can  be  normalized  to  the  total  number  of  RRUs  per
Master subframe. Also, this number can be dynamically specified by policy issued by the RAIS via the BSIS
(15.7).

15.4.5.2 Payoff calculation

This subclause provides an example of how the payoff in 15.4.5.1.2 can be calculated. This method is an
example and the implementation is vendor specific.

At each iteration, the offerer BS calculates the payoff (Payoff_requester) corresponding to each remaining
requester as follows:

— Payoff_requester  =  Requester_bid_update*  Rented_resource_amount*[T_renting_subframe

*(Renting_in_end_time – Renting_in_start_time)/CX_Frame_duration]/RRU_duration.

— The  offerer  selects  the  requesters  that  maximise  jointly  sum(Rented_resource_amount)  and

sum(Payoff_requester) over all the remaining requesters.

— The offerer BS derives the Minimal_payoff and Maximal_payoff from the selected requesters and

sends this information to all initial remaining requesters.

— Based on this information, each requester knows whether it has been selected or not by comparing

its own Payoff_requester with Minimal_payoff.

15.4.5.3 Inter-BSs communications for CT-CXP

The CT-CXP requires BS-to-BS communication between different systems. These inter-BS communications
are necessary to exchange the parameters related to the CT-CXP procedures described in 15.4.5.1.

The parameters related to CT-CXP are stored into the BSIS and into the database of each WirelessMAN-CX
BS of the shared distributed system architecture (see 15.1.5).

The exchange of these parameters between BSs is supported through network inter-BS communications for
the negotiated and non-negotiated modes. The related primitives are defined in 15.6.

The exchange of these parameters and related primitives (15.6) between BSs is also supported with over-the-
air MAC messages for the non-negotiated mode. These CXP messages are encapsulated within the CX-REQ
and CX-RSP MAC messages defined in 6.3.2.3. Intersystem over-the-air communications mechanisms are
detailed within 15.5.

15.5 Intersystem over-the-air communications

15.5.1 Procedure of intersystem communication over air

When  a  BS  needs  to  send  messages  to  its  neighbor  BS  over-the-air,  it  may  select  one  or  more  SSs  as
forwarders. The forwarding SSs are always the SSs which are in an overlap area between two BSs. These
SSs communicate with serving BS during the serving BS’s Master subframe.

System may select the forwarding SS according to the RSSI of neighbor BS detected by the interference
victim SSs. The SSs with the higher neighbor BS RSSI may be better.

After  identifying  the  forwarding  SS,  the  serving  BS  may  request  access  to  the  neighbor  BS  through  the
forwarding SS with the CX-ACCESS-NBS-REQ message. Upon receiving the access neighbor BS request,
the forwarding SS should try to access each neighbor BS during the Master subframe of that BS. It should
try  to  establish  synchronization  with  neighbor  BS,  obtain  transmission  parameters,  perform  ranging,
negotiate basic capabilities, be authorized and exchange encryption keys, and perform registration. These
procedures  should  be  performed  during  the  neighbor  BS’s  Master  subframe.  The  forwarding  SS  should
follow  a  procedure  similar  to  the  normal  network  entry  described  in  6.3.9,  except  that  in  the  RNG-REQ

Authorized licensed use limited to: John Greninger. Downloaded on April 01,2019 at 05:32:44 UTC from IEEE Xplore.  Restrictions apply.

2487
Copyright © 2018 IEEE. All rights reserved.

IEEE Std 802.16-2017
IEEE Standard for Air Interface for Broadband Wireless Access Systems

message, the forwarding SS should include the parameter “SS attribute” and the BSID of its serving BS via
the parameter “Serving BSID.” The neighbor BS may allocate Basic CID, primary management CID, and
secondary management CID to the forwarding SS.

In the DCD message, the neighbor BS shall indicate the frame used as Master.

If the forwarding SS fails to access the neighbor BS, it shall respond to its serving BS with an CX-ACCESS-
NBS-RSP message that includes the parameter “SS has failed to access the requested neighbor BS.” The
serving BS should select another SS as forwarding SS or terminate intersystem communication procedure
over air.

If the forwarding SS accesses the neighbor BS  successfully, it shall respond with an CX-ACCESS-NBS-
RSP message that includes the parameter '“SS has successfully accessed the requested neighbor BS.” The
serving BS and its neighbor BS can communicate with each other via the forwarding SS. The forwarding SS
should  communicate  with  the  serving  BS  during  serving  BS’s  Master  subframe  and  communicate  with
neighbor  BS  during  neighbor  BS’s  Master  subframe  during  the  intersystem  communication  period.  The
forwarding SS shall maintain corresponding contexts for both serving BS and neighbor BS.

Forward message request (by CX-FWD-REQ message) may be initiated by the serving BS or the neighbor
BS.

If the forward message is initiated by the serving BS, the serving BS should send forward request message to
the forwarding SS. After receiving forward request message from the serving BS, the forwarding SS should
send  a  response  signal  to  its  serving  BS.  The  forwarding  SS  should  ask  its  neighbor  BS  for  uplink
transmission opportunity and transmit messages to the neighbor BS during the allocated uplink transmission
resource. After  receiving the  forward  request message (by  CX-FWD-REQ  message)  from  the  forwarding
SS,  the  neighbor  may  send  a  response  (by  CX-FWD-RSP  message)  to  the  forwarding  SS.  The  forward
procedure initiated by the neighbor BS may follow similar procedure.

The serving and neighboring BSs may request that the forwarding SS forwards one or more messages to its
neighboring BS. During the intersystem communication procedure, the forwarding SS should perform the
ranging procedures (as described in 6.3.10) with the neighbor BS using its Master subframe.

When the intersystem communication ends, the serving BS or the neighbor BS may send a Forward End
Request message to the forwarding SS. After receiving the Forward End Request message, the forwarding
SS and neighbor BS may release all the contexts related to intersystem communication.

Figure 15-41 gives an example of intersystem communication procedure.

15.5.2 CT-CXP

Figure 15-42 describes the over-the-air communications messages between the offerer and requester for CT-
CXP operations. The messages between the offerer BS and requester BSs are conveyed through SS(s) acting
as forwarder between the offerer and requester BSs. Each forwarding SS is associated with the requester BS
and  is  in  the  overlapping  coverage  of  the  offerer  and  requester  BSs. The  forwarding  SS  can  receive  and
decode messages from both its serving BS (requester BS) and the foreign BS (offerer BS), and can transmit
messages to both offerer and requester BS.

The CT-CX-ADPD message is sent from the home requester BS to its associated forwarding SSs as a regular
multicast data message. The purpose of CT-CX-ADPD is to instruct the attitude of each forwarding SS when
it  receives  the  CT-CX-ADV-REQ  message.  CT-CX-ADPD  specifies  whether  the  forwarding  SS  has  to
forward the CT-CX-ADV-REQ message toward its serving BS (requester BS). If the content CT-CX-ADV-
REQ message meets the requirements instructed in CT-CX-ADPD, the forwarding SS actually forwards CT-
CX-ADV-REQ message from the offerer BS to its serving BS (requester BS). Otherwise, it does not. That
way,  CT-CX-ADPD  rules  the  transmissions  from  any  forwarding  SS  towards  its  serving  BS.  This
mechanism avoids having unnecessary transmissions from the forwarding SS towards its serving BS when
the renting conditions proposal specified in CT-CX-ADV-REQ does not meet the requester BS’s need. Any
policy can be established and can be adapted dynamically in time by the requester.

The CT-CX-ADV-REQ message is sent to the forwarding SS through regular data transmissions. If the CT-
CX-ADV-REQ  content  meets  the  CT-CX-ADPD  requirements,  the  forwarding  SS  forwards  the  CT-CX-
ADV-REQ  message  towards  its  serving  BS  according  to  the  mechanisms  specified  in  15.5.1.  In  order  to
ensure  the  CT-CX-ADV-REQ  message  is  appropriately  received  by  the  requester  BS,  CT-CX-ADV-REQ
message can be sent out by several forwarding SSs. If multiple CT-CX-ADV-REQ messages are received
from different forwarding SSs, the requester BS selects only one forwarding SS to complete the remaining
CT-CXP  operations  (CT-CX-ADV-RSP,  CT-CX-RA-REQ,  CT-CX-RA-RSP).  For  that,  the  requester  BS
notifies (with CT-CX-NTF message) each forwarding SS whether or not it should complete the remaining

CT-CXP  operations.  Once  the  selected  forwarding  SS  has  received  the  CT-CX-ACK  message  from  the
offerer  BS,  it  forwards  this  message  to  its  serving  BS  (requester)  to  confirm  that  the  requester  BS  can
actually use the rented resources for the agreed renting period with the offerer BS.

During  the  initial  phase,  as  previously  mentioned,  in  case  the  renting  conditions  sent  in  CT-CX-ADAP
message are not met, the forwarding SS does not forward the CT-CX-ADV-REQ message to its serving BS
(requester). However, upon requester BS recommendation (policy-based), even if the renting conditions are
not met, the requester BS can allow the forwarding SS to convey the information about the list of channel
LC (parameter included in CT-CX-ADV-REQ). This information will provide the serving BS some further
information about other radio resources renting opportunities on other channel (frequency domain).

Whole CT-CXP procedures are detailed in 15.4.5.

15.5.3 MAC messages for intersystem communication over-the-air

CX-FWD-REQ and CX-FWD-RSP MAC messages are used for intersystem communication over-the-air.
The  SS  in  the  overlapped  area  of  two  systems  can  be  used  as  the  forwarder  for  the  intersystem
communication over-the-air. The forwarding SS shall forward the CX-FWD-REQ messages sent from the
source BS to the destination BS and transmit the CX-FWD-RSP message sent from the destination BS to
source BS. If the connection ID in the intersystem coexistence message is broadcast CID, all the serving SS
may be the forwarding SS if the specific SS can communicate with a neighbor BS.

The  Action  Code  in  the  CX-FWD-REQ  and  CX-FWD-RSP  is  used  to  identify  the  corresponding
coexistence action. intersystem communication messages with different Action Codes may contain different
TLV encoded attributes. Table 15-6 shows the encoding of each coexistence action.

15.5.3.1 CX-FWD-REQ [Action Code: Base Station Descriptor (BSD)]

The BSD-related attributes contain the information characteristic for the base station. This message is sent
by  a  BS  during  the  subchannel  2  and  subchannel  4,  every  CXCC  repetition  period.  In  subchannel  2  the
message shall be sent in the CX_CMI_D(n) slot of the CXCC (see 15.3.3.2, 15.3.1.2.2) claimed by the base
station. It is intended to be decoded as intelligible interference by subscriber stations associated with other
systems (see 15.3.3.4). The CX-FWD-REQ with Action Type=BSD is also sent on an occasional basis in the
CX_CMI_D(4) slot. In subchannel 4, this message is sent in the first cycle of the CXCC multi-frame.

The BSD attributes contain pertinent information related to the base station, allowing foreign (interfered-
with) subscriber stations to identify it as interference.

The  CX-FWD-REQ  message  containing  the  BSD  attributes  also  contains  a  UL_MAP  message,  directing
CX- FWD-REQ (Action type=SSURF) messages (15.6.1.4) to the complementary CX_CMI_U(n) slot.

15.5.3.2 CX-FWD-REQ [Action Code: Subscriber Station Uplink Radio Frequency (SSURF)]

The Subscriber Station Uplink Radio Frequency (SSURF) message is transmitted as a CX-FWD-REQ MAC
message. The Subscriber Station Uplink Radio Frequency (SSURF) message is the complement to the BSD
message  except  it  is  sent  on  the  uplink  during  the  CMI  claimed  by  the  base  station  to  which  the  SS  is
registered or during the uplink Master subframe of the CXCC subchannel 4.

If used on CXCC subchannel 2, the CX-FWD-REQ message, when received by foreign (interfered-with)
base stations, should identify the SS as being an interferer (15.3.3.5).

The SS sending this message shall not expect a response.

message was sent; usually the maximum allowable EIRP for the
operation of this station.

15.5.3.3 CX-FWD-REQ [Action Code: CT-CXP Advertisement Request (CT-CX-ADV-REQ)]

The CT-CX-ADV-REQ message is transmitted as a CX-FWD-REQ MAC message. This message specifies
the advertisement discovery information sent out by the offerer BS towards the forwarding SSs (associated
to requester BSs and located in the overlapping area of this offerer system and the surrounding requester
systems) when CT-CXP operation is over-the-air. The CT-CX-ADV-REQ message is sent by the offerer BS
within  the  mechanisms  specified  in  15.5.2.  If  the  CT-CX-ADV-REQ  message  content  meets  the  CT-CX-
ADPD requirements, the forwarding SS forwards the CT-CX-ADV-REQ message towards its serving BS
following mechanisms specified in 15.5.2. CT-CX-ADV-REQ message provides the necessary information
to these forwarding SSs to enable them to inform their home BS (requester) about radio resource sharing
opportunities proposed by the offerer BS.

15.5.3.4 CX-FWD-RSP [Action Code: CT-CXP Advertisement Response (CT-CX-ADV-RSP)]

The CT-CX-ADV-RSP message is transmitted as a CX-FWD-RSP MAC message. In response to the CT-
CX-ADV-REQ message,  and if the  forwarding SS has  been  selected to complete  the  CT-CXP operations
(specified in the CT-CX-NTF message), the forwarding SS responds to the offerer with an CT-CX-ADV-
RSP message mentioning its interest to rent all or a fraction of the resource offered by the offerer for the
total or a portion of the proposed renting period (Renting_out_start_time, Renting_out_send_time). The CT-
CX-ADV-RSP  message  content  is  aligned  with  renting  requirements  specified  within  the  CT-CX-ADPD
message. The  CT-CX-ADV-RSP  message  is  sent  by  the  forwarding  SS  within  the  time  interval  and  with
mechanisms specified in 15.5.2.

provides  to  the  requester  some  information  about  the  BSIDs  of  the  members  of  its  own  community. The
detailed process is described within 15.4.5. The CT-CX-RA-REQ message is sent by the offerer BS with
mechanisms specified in 15.5.2.

The CT-CX-ADPD message is transmitted as a CX-FWD-REQ MAC message. CT-CX-ADPD message is

forwarding  SS  when  the  forwarding  SS  receives  CT-CX-ADV-REQ  message.  CT-CX-ADPD  specifies
whether the forwarding SS has to forward a CT-CX-ADV-REQ message toward its serving BS (requester

15.5.3.8 CX-FWD-REQ [Action Code: CT-CXP Acknowledgment (CT-CX-ACK)]

The CT-CX-ACK message is transmitted as a CX-FWD-REQ MAC message. The offerer BS acknowledges
the reception of the CT-CX-RA-REQ message with the CT-CX-ACK message. The CT-CX-ACK message
is sent by the offerer BS with mechanisms specified in 15.5.2. The forwarding SS forwards this message to
its serving BS (requester) with a regular data message to confirm that the requester BS can actually use the
rented resources for the agreed renting period with the offerer BS.

15.5.3.9 CX-FWD-RSP [Action Code: CT-CXP Notification (CT-CX-NTF)]

The CT-CX-NTF message is transmitted as a CX-FWD-RSP MAC message. In order to ensure the CT-CX-
ADV-REQ  is  appropriately  received  by  the  requester  BS,  CT-CX-ADV-REQ  can  be  sent  out  by  several
forwarding  SSs  for  the  CT-CXP  operations.  If  multiple  CT-CX-ADV-REQ  messages  are  received  from
different forwarding SSs, the requester BS selects only one forwarding SS to complete the remaining CT-
CXP operations (CT-CX-ADV-RSP message, CT-CX-RA-REQ, CT-CX-RA-RSP). For that, the offerer BS
indicates  to  (through  CT-CX-NTF)  each  of  the  forwarding  SSs  whether  or  not  it  should  complete  the
remaining CT-CXP operations. The CT-CX-NTF message is a regular data message.

The following parameters shall be included in the CX-FWD-RSP (Action Code = CT-CX-NTF) message:

TLV parameter name

Notes

Notification Bit Flag (NBF)

This flag indicates whether the forwarding SS is selected to complete the
CT-CXP operations.

coexistence neighbor BS to request to add it to coexistence neighbor list. The following parameters shall be

Notes

The channel information of the requesting BS, including modulation
mode, and alternative channel flag.

15.5.3.11 CX-FWD-RSP (Action Code: Add Neighbor Response)

The CX-FWD-RSP message with Action Code = Add Neighbor Response is sent by the BS to respond to the
Add Coexistence Neighbor Request.

A CX-FWD-RSP message having Add Neighbor Response as Action Code has no TLV parameters.

15.5.3.12 CX-FWD-REQ (Action Code: Delete Neighbor Request)

The  CX-FWD-RSP  message  with  Action  Code  =  Delete  Neighbor  Request  is  sent  by  the  BS  to  the
coexistence neighbor BS to request deletion from its coexistence neighbor list.

A CX-FWD-REQ message having Delete Neighbor Request as its Action Code has no TLV parameters.

15.5.3.13 CX-FWD-RSP (Action code: Delete Neighbor Response)

The CX-FWD-RSP message with Action Code = Delete Neighbor Response is sent by the BS to respond to
the  CX-FWD-REQ  message  with Action  Code  =  Delete  Neighbor  Request.  A  CX-FWD-RSP  message
having delete neighbor response as Action Code has no TLV parameters.

15.5.3.16 CX-FWD-REQ (Action Code: Evaluate Interference Request)

The CX-FWD-REQ (Action Code: Evaluate Interference Request) message is used by a BS for requesting
other BSs in the community to either transmit their Interference Evaluation Bursts or to be silent, in order to
coordinate  their  operation  during  this  measurement.  This  measurement  allows  evaluating  the  maximum
aggregated co-channel and adjacent channel interference. The message is sent to every base station in the
community, indicating either the request to send the Interference Evaluation Burst or to insert a GAP DIUC/
UIUC interval for the duration of the Interference Evaluation Burst. The Interference Evaluation Burst may
be transmitted by the BS or by the associated SSs. When the Interference Evaluation Burst is transmitted by
the BS, which is denoted as IEBBS, there are 20 different Interference Evaluation Bursts to choose from,
which may differ due to Beam Forming or power concentration on specific subchannels.

The various Interference Evaluation Bursts of a BS transmitted by the BS are identified by the configuration
number.  The  various  Interference  Evaluation  Bursts  of  a  SS  transmitted  by  the  SS  are  identified  by  the
IEBSS number, which runs from 1 to 199. The message indicates the MAC Frame number, the offset from
its start and the duration of the requested Interference Evaluation Burst time slot. A number of Interference
Evaluation  Bursts  may  be  concatenated,  under  the  constraint  that  their  total  duration,  including  the
propagation delays, does not exceed the total allocation duration. It is recommended that this duration will
be lower than 1 ms. The time slot shall use the DL subframe for BS Interference Evaluation Bursts and UL
subframe  for  SS  Interference  Evaluation  Bursts.  The  Interference  Evaluation  Burst  should  be  transmitted
using the operational characteristics of the radio behavior.

The following parameters shall be included in this message with one exception. When this message requests
that a BS insert a Gap DIUC/UIUC interval, the parameters specifying the transmission of the Interference
Evaluation Burst shall not be included in the message.

GPS_LOC

The GPS_LOC of the requesting BS.

the Interference Evaluation Burst.

Bursts in a time slot.
Each Interference Evaluation Burst is listed in a Two field

15.5.3.18 CX-FWD-REQ (Action Code: Work as Slave Request)

A message sent by a new BS to request use of an existing Master subframe, to a BS already acting as Master
in the specific subframe. The Master BS should evaluate the interference caused by the requesting BS before
answering the request. However the Master BS may also directly respond to the request. If more than one
base station is using the subframe as Master, the IBS should send this message to every BS separately.

The Interference Evaluation Burst transmitted during the claimed Master subframe should consist of a DL
subframe, starting with the first zone using the mandatory permutation (if applicable) and continuing with
other used zones and their permutations. Each zone should be transmitted using the operational power.

15.5.3.22 CX-FWD-REQ (Action Code: CMI Interference Indication)

The CX-FWD-REQ message with Action Code = CMI Interference Indication is sent by the BS to indicate
the intensity and type of interference it is receiving as a system. The information content of this message is
derived  from  foreign  SSURF  and  BSD  messages  received  by  the  system.  Non-WirelessMAN-CX
interference detected by the system is similarly reported. The message specifies the threshold of interference
sensitivity of the victim BS or SS, and assigns a CCID report number to specific sources of interference,
allowing  higher  levels  of  the  CX  protocol  to  track  the  resolution  or  mitigation  of  the  interference  to  the
victim terminals.

15.5.3.23 CX-FWD-RSP (Action Code: CMI Interference Resolution)

The CX-FWD-RSP message with Action Code = CMI Interference Resolution is sent to the BS generating
the  CX-FWD-REQ  message  with  Action  Code  =  CMI  Interference  Indication.  This  message  sets  the
threshold of interference detection at the victim device and indicates to that device the status of interference
resolution. Other actions related to the Coexistence Protocol and interference mitigation may be taken as
well and may precede and/or preclude the sending of this message. Such actions may be related to CINR
measurements and other channel quality assessments or involve rapid channel changes as a result of primary
user requirements.

The  following  parameters  shall  be  included  in  the  CX-FWD-RSP  (Action  Code  =  CMI  Interference
Resolution) message:

TLV parameter name

Notes

Interference Victim Device Identity

BSID or SSID of victim device(s).

CCID

Interference report number to which this message applies.

Inhibition Period Set

Inhibit interference report of device by given number of CXCC cycles.

Interference Threshold Set

Set interference threshold of device to given level.

Interference Incidence count cycles

The number of CXCC cycles in which there was an interference
incidence.

Interference Resolution Status

Resolution of interference to which stated CCID applies: resolved/
tolerated/pending.

The C-CX-REQ primitive shall include the following parameters:

silently discarded.

— TLV Encoded Attributes: Each coexistence primitive Action Type has its own set of required and
optional  attributes.  Unless  explicitly  stated,  there  is  no  requirement  on  the  ordering  of  attributes
within  a  C-CX-REQ  primitive. The TLV  encoded  attributes  values  are  defined  in  Table 11-76  of
11.30.

15.6.1.2 C-CX-REQ (Action_Type = Evaluate Interference)

15.6.1.2.1 Function

This primitive is used by a BS to request other BSs in the community to either transmit their Interference
Evaluation  Bursts  or  to  be  silent,  in  order  to  coordinate  their  operation  during  this  measurement.  This
measurement allows the maximum aggregated co-channel and adjacent channel interference to be evaluated.
The  message  is  sent  to  every  base  station  in  the  community,  indicating  either  a  request  to  send  the
Interference  Evaluation  Burst  or  to  insert  GAP  DIUC/UIUC  interval  for  the  duration  of  the  Interference
Evaluation Burst. The Interference Evaluation Burst may be transmitted by the BS or by the associated SSs.
In case of the Interference Evaluation Burst transmission by the BS, which is denoted as IEBBS, 20 different
Interference Evaluation Bursts are defined, which may differ due to Beam Forming or power concentration
on specific subchannels. The various Interference Evaluation Bursts transmitted by the BS are identified by
the configuration number. The various Interference Evaluation Bursts transmitted by the SS are identified by
the IEBSS number, which runs from 1 to 199. The message is indicating the MAC Frame number, the offset
from  its  start  and  the  duration  of  the  requested  Interference  Evaluation  Burst  time  slot.  A  number  of
Interference Evaluation Bursts may be concatenated, under the constraint that their total duration, including
the propagation delays, does not exceed the total time slot duration. It is recommended that this duration
should be lower than 1 ms. The time slot shall use the DL subframe for BS Interference Evaluation Bursts
and  UL  subframe  for  SS  Interference  Evaluation  Bursts.  The  Interference  Evaluation  Burst  should  be
transmitted using the operational characteristics of the radio behavior.

If  a  specific  BS  is  requested  to  insert  a  GAP/DIUC,  the  parameters  specifying  the  transmission  of  the
Interference Evaluation Burst shall not be sent.

15.6.1.3 C-CX-REQ (Action_Type = Work as Slave)

15.6.1.3.1 Function

This primitive is used by a new BS to request the use of an existing Master subframe as Slave. In general, the
Master BS should evaluate the interference created by the requesting BS before answering this request. If
more than one base station is using the subframe as Master, the IBS should send this message to every BS
separately. The Master BS should evaluate the interference caused by the requesting BS before answering
the request. However, the Master BS may also directly respond to the request.

The  Interference  Evaluation  Burst  should  be  transmitted  during  the  claimed  Master  subframe  and  should
consist of a DL subframe, starting with the first zone using the mandatory permutation (if applicable) and
continuing  with  other  used  zones  and  their  permutations.  Each  zone  should  be  transmitted  using  the
operational power.

15.6.1.5.3 When generated

This primitive is sent by the victim BS to indicate the intensity and type of interference it is receiving as a
system. The information content of this primitive is derived from foreign SSURF and BSD messages the
system  receives.  Non-WirelessMAN-CX  interference  detected  by  the  system  is  similarly  reported.  The
primitive specifies the threshold of interference sensitivity of the victim BS or SS and assigns a CCID report
number to specific sources of interference, allowing higher levels of the CX protocol to track the resolution
or mitigation of the interference to the victim terminals.

15.6.1.5.4 Effect of receipt

This primitive is received by the interfering base station or by the NCMS. The primitive should result in
alterations  to  the  signals  that  originally  created  the  identified  interference  (for  example,  by  changing  the
EIRP, scheduling, or emission characteristics of the interference emitter). If the interference is created by
other sources, for example, by primary users, other actions such as a channel change may be implemented.

Pricing_Bit_Flag (PBF)

This field is used only with backhaul-based inter BS

before reuse.

15.6.1.8 C-CX-REQ (Action_Type = Token Negotiation)

15.6.1.8.1 Function

This primitive is used by an IEEE 802.16 entity (offering BS) or NCMS only if NMBF = 1 (i.e., when the
negotiation mode is active). At each iteration of the negotiation, the decision making algorithm applied by
the offerer derives a minimum and maximal payoff based on the requesters’ bids. At each of these iterations,
updated values of these payoffs are provided by the offerer to the requesters still bidding for the renting.

15.6.1.9 C-CX-REQ (Action_Type = Token Resource Allocation)

15.6.1.9.1 Function

After the negotiation is complete, this primitive is used by an IEEE 802.16 entity (offering BS) or NCMS to
inform  each  requester  whether  the  resource  it  bidded  for  has  been  granted.  Each  granted  requester  is
informed about the credit token clearing price necessary to complete the CT-CX operations. Derived from
the selection process, the clearing price corresponds to the number of credit tokens per RRU that has to be
considered by the selected renter to derive the total number of credit tokens to be considered in the pricing
method specified within PBF flag of CT-CX-REQ (token-based resource sharing advertisement) message.

15.6.2 C-CX-RSP

This primitive is used by an IEEE 802.16 entity or NCMS to respond a request in coexistence procedure.
The Action_Type included in this primitive defines the type of coexistence procedure to be performed. The
possible Action_Types for this primitive are listed in the table below:

parameters.

The C-CX-RSP primitive shall include the following parameters:

— Action  Type:  The  Action  Type  is  one  byte  in  length,  and  identifies  the  type  of  coexistence
procedure  to  be performed. When a  primitive is  received with an  invalid Action Type,  it  shall  be
silently discarded.

— TLV Encoded Attributes: Each coexistence primitive Action Type has its own set of required and
optional  attributes.  Unless  explicitly  stated,  there  is  no  requirement  on  the  ordering  of  attributes
within  a  C-CX-RSP  primitive.  The  TLV  encoded  attributes  values  are  defined  in  Table 11-76  of
11.30.

The following subclauses define the primitive when its action type is set to a specific action.

15.7 Network-based identification of specific spectrum services or applications

15.7.1 Overview

The  method  described  below  allows  identifying  specific  (protected)  spectrum  users  based  on  their
GPS_LOC and the geographic protection area, as defined by the national regulations. Such spectrum users,
during their activity period at a specific location, register themselves with a database of the National Radio
Administration and indicated the range of used frequencies and the requested time intervals for protection.
The registration can use a WEB application, above the scope of this document.

BWA base  stations  register  themselves  with  the  same  database. The list  of  the provided attributes  should
include the following elements:

— GPS location
— Network address
— Tx power
— List including N structures for N channels described as follows:

— Center frequency of the transmit channel i (both FDD and TDD)
— Channel width of channel i
— ACLR (Adjacent Channel Leakage Ratio)
— ACLR in the 2nd adjacent channel
— Center frequency of the receive channel j, if FDD is used
— Bandwidth of channel j

— Antenna type and direction
— Noise power

The list of the parameters to be provided by the SSU should include the following:

— Radio application identification
— GPS location of the center of the protection area (not necessarily the GPS location of its operation)
— Required radius of the protection area (optional)
— Tx power
— List including N structures for N channels described as follows:

— Center frequency of the transmit channel i (both FDD and TDD)
— Channel width of channel i
— ACLR of channel i
— ACLR in the 2nd adjacent channel to channel i
— Center frequency of the receive channel j, if FDD is used
— Bandwidth of channel j

— Antenna type and direction
— Noise power
— Date and absolute time of requested operation start
— Duration  of  operation;  for  systems  using  special  signaling  procedures  the  duration  should  be

maximum four hours. In case of longer operation, the spectrum request shall be renewed.

A special application, running on the Radio Administration Server, should identify the limitations imposed
to the BWA applications, regarding the following:

— Operating frequency channels
— Transmit power
— Time constraints

15.7.2 Architecture

The proposed architecture uses the Radio Application Identification Server (RAIS) for the devices providing
specific radio applications. Generally the RAIS will be provided by the National Radio Administration. The
communication of the BS with the RAIS is secured by VPN or other procedures.

The  RAIS  has  connections  with  the  BWA  base  stations,  but  also  with  base  stations  providing  TV
applications, Satellite applications, Military applications, Health applications, Security applications, etc.

A special class is the Ad-Hoc protected applications, as wireless microphones or TV vehicle transmissions,
which  are  mobile  ad-hoc  protected  applications.  In  this  situation,  a  secure  communication  should  be
established between a Laptop with cellular interface or a hand-held device and the RAIS.

The RAIS has connections with the BWA base stations also serves for the administration of the credit tokens
to  be  used  by  the  BWA  base  stations.  For  that  purpose,  RAIS  can  specify  to  BWA  base  stations  some
policies  (ruling)  for  the  usage  of  the  credit  tokens  by  the  BWA  base  stations  covered  by  this  RAIS.  For
example, polices can specify the number of credit tokens to be assigned to each BWA base stations at some
given locations or some given time periods, the negotiation mode, the pricing method, and so forth.

15.7.3 Operation

When  a  change  of  the  spectrum  usage  or  an  update  is  necessary,  the  RAIS  should  use  the  C-CX-REQ
primitive with Action_Type= Frequency Channel Avoidance to the affected BSs with the request to change
the operating frequency and eventually with a recommendation for the new operating frequencies. From this
moment all the operators in the frequency range will share the available spectrum, following procedures to
be agreed or those defined by WirelessMAN-CX.

The  BS  should  inform  the  RAIS  about  the  availability  of  the  requested  frequency  channel,  by  using  the
primitive C-CX-RSP (Action_Type= Frequency Channel Avoidance).

An HR-BS may operate as a relay station to a serving HR-BS.

An HR-BS acting as RS mode operates in either TTR mode or STR mode.

The procedure for mode change consists of following activities:

applies to both STR and TTR relay modes.

When supporting STR relay mode, the affected HR-BS maintains base station functionality.

The  HR-BS  having  no  connection  to  backhaul  transmits  MM-ADV  message  with  action  type  =  0b0100

service with an available backhaul link.

TTR or STR mode. In response to MM-RS-REQ, the superordinate HR-BS transmits MM-RS-RSP message

MM-RS-RSP message, the affected HR-BS starts establishing the relay link with the superordinate HR-BS
immediately or retransmits another MM-RS-REQ message at the action time. If the superordinate HR-BS
rejects  the  request,  the  superordinate  HR-BS  informs  the  HR-BS  having  no  connection  to  backhaul  the
rejection of the request. Upon receiving the MM-RS-RSP message with rejection information, the HR-BS
either tries to establish relay link with another HR-BS or follows the standalone network operation described
in 16.4.

To support handover as a part of robustness against SPOF as described in 16.6, an indication of whether
MAC  context  information  of  the  subordinate  HR-MS  is  being  shared  by  infrastructure  stations  shall  be
transmitted to HR-MS.

16.1.1.2 Relay link configuration

When establishing the relay link, the superordinate HR-BS transmits RS_Config-CMD message described
in 6.3.2.3.63 to configure PHY parameter set including Frame Number Action indicating the time to start
acting as HR-RS.

While the superordinate HR-BS is maintaining the relay link, the superordinate HR-BS shall send R-link
channel descriptor (RCD) message described in 6.3.2.3.60 in the DL relay zone. The superordinate HR-BS
also  shall  send  RS_Config-CMD  message  in  the  DL  relay  zone  when  PHY  parameter  needs  to  be
reconfigured.

The  HR-BS  acting  as  relay  may  transmit  MM-ADV  message  with  action  type=0b0000  described  in
6.3.2.3.102.1 for its subordinate MSs to update PHY/MAC parameter after receiving RCD or RS_Config-
CMD message.

16.1.1.3 Relay link release

When  the  affected  HR-BS  recovers  the  backhaul  link,  the  notification  of  recovery  is  announced  to  the
backhaul  network  or  its  superordinate  HR-BS  through  the  backhaul  interface.  The  superordinate  HR-BS
may then initiate HR-MS handover back to the recovered HR-BS. The recovered HR-BS may have been
storing MAC context information of the serving MSs (e.g., basic capabilities, security capabilities). Such
context information allows HR-MS to perform optimized network reentry when returning back to the HR-
BS upon its recovery.

The affected HR-BS transmits the MM-ADV message with action type = 0b0101 described in 6.3.2.3.102.1
including expected time of backhaul recovery. When receiving the MM-ADV message, HR-MS performs
either handover to neighbor infrastructure station and returns to the HR-BS at the expected time or wait until
restarting service with available backhaul link.

If the HR-BS acting as relay receives the request of relay link release from superordinate HR-BS but the
HR-BS acting as relay does not recover the backhaul link, the HR-BS either tries to establish relay link with
another HR-BS that has the backhaul link as described in 16.1.1 or follows standalone network operation
described in 16.4.

16.1.2 Relay function for HR-MS

An  HR-MS  may  operate  as  an  HR-RS  to  provide  connectivity  for  multiple  out-of-coverage  HR-MSs.
During basic capability negotiation at network entry, an HR-MS that is capable of role change to HR-RS
shall report such capability to the superordinate HR-BS/HR-RS. A mode switch to HR-RS shall be initiated
by its superordinate HR-BS.

In response to MM-RS-REQ, the HR-MS transmits the MM-RS-RSP message described in 6.3.2.3.102.6.

To establish relay link with an HR-BS, HR-MS having a role as HR-RS transmits MM-RS-REQ message

either tries to establish relay link with another HR-BS or follows base station function described in 16.1.3.

While HR-MS is acting as relay mode, the superordinate HR-BS may send an RCD message to configure
the  Relay  operation  parameters  as  specified  in  6.3.9.18.  The  HR-BS  also  shall  send  RS-Config-CMD
message in the DL relay zone when PHY layer parameter needs to be reconfigured.

HR-MS acting as relay mode may transmit MM-ADV message described in 6.3.2.3.102.1 to update PHY/
MAC layer parameter after receiving RCD or RS-Config-CMD message.

16.1.2.3 Dual-role operation of HR-MS

An HR-MS acting as RS may maintain MS functionalities in company with RS functionalities. When an
HR-MS in connected state receives RS_Config-CMD message, the HR-MS establishes relay link with the
superordinate HR-BS and starts the RS mode. At this time, the MS mode in the HR-MS is behaving as a
subordinate  station  of  the  RS  mode.  For  connecting  the  MS’s  service  flow(s),  the  MS  mode  shall
communicate with the RS mode through internal interfaces in the dual-role HR-MS. The RS mode in the
dual-role  HR-MS  requests  to  the  superordinate  HR-BS  for  switching  the  data  path  of  the  MS  mode  by
exchanging the MS_Context-REQ/RSP message, as if the MS’s handover process had been performed.

16.1.2.4 Relay link release

An HR-MS acting as RS may end its relay service and remove the relay link from the HR-BS. During the
HR-MS’s  relay  mode  release  process,  all  subordinate  HR-MSs  of  the  HR-MS  acting  as  RS  shall  be
transferred to another infrastructure station prior to HR-MS’s relay mode release. The HR-MS acting as RS
prevents HR-MS (re)entry and transmits MM-ADV message to transfer all subordinate HR-MSs to another
infrastructure  station.  An  HR-MS  acting  as  RS  may  transmit  an  MM-RL-REQ  message  described  in
6.3.2.3.102.7 in UL relay zone to an HR-BS so that it initiates the release procedure and requests handover
of all its subordinate HR-MSs. Upon receiving the MM-RL-REQ message, the HR-BS decides whether it
allows the HR-MS’s relay mode release. If the request is accepted, the HR-BS may transmit the MM-RL-
RSP  message  described  in  6.3.2.3.102.8  in  DL  relay  zone  to  inform  the  acceptance.  Upon  receiving  the
MM-RL-RSP message, the HR-MS acting as RS starts relay mode release process immediately or at action
time expires. If the HR-BS rejects the request, the HR-BS informs the HR-MS acting as RS the rejection of
the request by transmitting the MM-RL-RSP message in DL relay zone. Upon receiving the MM-RL-RSP
message  with  rejection  information,  the  HR-MS  acting  as  RS  continues  operating  in  relay  mode. After
action time expires, the HR-MS acting as RS retransmits an MM-RL-REQ message in UL relay zone to the
HR-BS.

The mode release process may be initiated by an HR-BS through transmitting an unsolicited MM-RL-RSP
message in DL relay zone.

After mode release process, all the relay-related connections and resources are released between the HR-BS
and the HR-MS.

If the HR-MS receives the request of relay link release from the serving HR-BS, the HR-BS either tries to
establish  relay  link  with  another  HR-BS  as  described  in  16.1.2.1  or  follows  the  base  station  function
described in 16.1.3.

16.1.3 Base station function for HR-MS

An HR-MS may operate as an HR-BS to provide connectivity for itself and other HR-MSs. The HR-MS
may start operating as an HR-BS in a Proactive operation or a Reactive operation.

In proactive operation, the mode change is directed by a superordinate HR-BS of the HR-MS. During basic
capability negotiation at network entry, an HR-MS that is capable of role change to HR-BS shall report such
capability to the superordinate HR-BS/HR-RS.

In reactive operation, the mode switch is initiated by the HR-MS itself.

While operating as an HR-BS, the station may maintain certain MS functionalities.

16.1.3.1 Proactive operation

A superordinate HR-BS may select a target HR-MS among its subordinate HR-MSs that are capable of role
changing to HR-BS, according to the measured signal power at HR-BS and/or subordinate HR-MSs’ status
information  such  as  the  battery  level.  The  superordinate  HR-BS  may  transmit  MM-ADV  message  with
action type set to 0b1000 for obtaining the status information of the subordinate HR-MSs. Upon receiving
the MM-ADV message with action type set to 0b1000, the subordinate HR-MS capable of role changing to
HR-BS  may  report  its  status  information  to  the  superordinate  HR-BS  via  MM-STAT-REP  message  as
described in 6.3.2.3.102.9.

After selecting the target HR-MS, the superordinate HR-BS requests the target HR-MS to change its mode
to  HR-BS  by  transmitting  MM-BS-REQ  message.  The  MM-BS-REQ  message  may  include  PHY
operational parameters recommended by the superordinate HR-BS. If the target HR-MS accepts the request

from the superordinate HR-BS to change the mode to HR-BS, it shall transmit MM-BS-RSP message to the
superordinate HR-BS when it is ready to start HR-BS role.

After receiving the MM-BS-RSP message, the superordinate HR-BS shall transmit MM-BS-CMD message
to  the  target  HR-MS  to  inform  the  action  time  for  starting  as  HR-BS  mode.  If  the  action  time  for  mode
change is included in the MM-BS-CMD message, the target HR-MS starts the HR-BS mode operation at the
expiration of the action time. At the same time, the superordinate HR-BS may stop the HR-BS role in order
to avoid potential interference from the target HR-MS.

If handover of subordinate MSs connected to the superordinate HR-BS is necessary, the superordinate HR-
BS may transmit MS_Context-REQ message that contains MS context information before sending MM-BS-
CMD message to the target HR-MS.

16.1.3.2 Reactive operation

The HR-MSs that are capable of role changing to HR-BS may contend for operating at BS mode when the
superordinate HR-BS fails. The HR-MSs may initiate a mode switch to HR-BS after expiration of a random
backoff timer to avoid potential collision among adjacent HR-MSs trying to perform a mode switch to HR-
BS at the same time.

After  completion  of  mode  switch,  the  HR-MS  acting  as  HR-BS  may  request  mode  change  to  one  of  its
subordinate HR-MSs in order to hand HR-BS role over. In this case, it follows the procedure for proactive
operation as described in 16.1.3.1.

16.1.3.2.1 Collision resolution

When multiple HR-MSs try to change their mode to HR-BS in the same coverage area, interference to each
other may occur. In order to avoid it, an HR-MS that tries to perform BS mode operation should transmit
preamble in a certain time period before changing the mode.

To resolve a collision that may occur during preamble transmissions by multiple HR-MSs, an HR-MS that
can act as an HR-BS changes its mode to HR-BS after going through two phases: initial access phase and
collision resolution phase. Basic channel access mechanism is based on CSMA/CA (Carrier Sense Multiple
Access/Collision Avoidance) protocol with backoff algorithm. Backoff slot time is defined as 5 ms, which is
identical to the frame size.

The initial access phase is as follows:

— HR-MS that can act as HR-BS calculates the value of backoff timer from a window [0, CW1].
— If a preamble from other HR-MS is detected prior to expiration of the backoff timer, the HR-MS

gives up its mode change.

— HR-MS  transmits  a  preamble  at  the  first  OFDM  symbol  duration  in  5 ms  frame  once  its  backoff

timer is expired.

— After transmitting a preamble, HR-MS goes into the collision resolution phase.

The collision resolution phase is as follows:

— HR-MS that has transmitted preamble successfully in the initial access phase selects the value of

backoff timer from a window [0, CW2] randomly in the manner of uniform distribution.

— If preamble from other HR-MS is detected prior to expiration of the backoff timer, the HR-MS gives

up its mode change.

— Since its backoff timer is expired the HR-MS starts BS mode operation.

CW1 and CW2 are predefined. The range of CW1 and CW2 is between 0 to 1024.

16.2 Support for direct communication between HR-MSs

16.2.1 General description

In HR-MS direct communication, data packets are exchanged between two HR-MSs directly or by passing
through another HR-MS. The two communicating HR-MSs are the source and the sink of data. The data
packets  are  passed from  upper layers  to  MAC at the source  HR-MS  and  back  to  upper layers  at the sink
HR-MS.

HR-MS direct communication is applicable when 1) the two HR-MSs are in coverage of and are directly
associated to an HR infrastructure station; 2) one HR-MS is in coverage of and directly associated to an HR
infrastructure station, while the other HR-MS is out of coverage of any HR infrastructure stations; 3) the two
HR-MSs are out of coverage of any HR infrastructure stations.

HR-MS direct communication using centralized resource allocation, also referred to as BS-controlled direct
communication, is described in 16.2.2.

HR-MS direct communication using distributed resource allocation among nearby HR-MSs, also referred to
as  talk-around  direct  communication,  is  described  in  16.2.3.  Resource  for  talk-around  HR-MS  direct
communication  may  be  allocated  in  a  distributed  manner  among  nearby  HR-MSs  independent  of
infrastructure node deployment.

16.2.2 HR-MS direct communication with centralized control

When HR-MSs are associated to an infrastructure station, resource for HR-MS direct communication can be
allocated by the HR infrastructure station.
